messages.subject: Naive follow-up question
messages.body_plain:
So our (numerically unstable, but mathematically pretty) BBVB algorithm in /feature/bbvb seems to be working.

I now understand that stan::model::gradient is powerful but not necessarily cheap to call. (I will factor this into our efforts towards developing a different/more scalable algorithm.)

My question: is model_.template log_prob() cheap to call?

More specifically: my ALP.stan model file goes through the magic box and I get ALP.cpp. Within is my beautiful log prob function with log det Jacobians, etc. I can call that guy and only pay the price of evaluating the function, right? That whole process of .stan -> .cpp (or any other expensive procedure behind the scenes) is only done ONCE, correct?

Sorry for these naive questions! You guys have been super helpful.

Cheers,
Alp

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Naive follow-up question
messages.body_plain:
On Aug 1, 2014, at 8:45 AM, Alp Kucukelbir <akucu...@gmail.com> wrote:

> So our (numerically unstable, but mathematically pretty) BBVB algorithm in /feature/bbvb seems to be working.

That's fantastic news.  I'm so glad you're sticking with this.

> I now understand that stan::model::gradient is powerful but not necessarily cheap to call. (I will factor this into our efforts towards developing a different/more scalable algorithm.)

If you profile either the optimizer or our HMC implementation,
almost all the time's spent in calculating gradients.

> My question: is model_.template log_prob() cheap to call?

That depends on the template parameters.  If they're double and
not propto, then it's just the evaluation without dropping any
const terms and should be relatively fast.

If you want the same propto calc (dropping constant terms) you
get with calling it with true,true with autodiff vars the way
gradient does, then it's quite a bit more expensive than just
calling the function with doubles, but not as expensive as doing
the autodiff tree.  The expression tree gets built up, but not used.
There's no way around that with the way we have the constant-dropping
implemented.  It'd be great if we could refine the propto thing to
work with double input, but it'd be a huge amount of work.  The way
to build it would be to add template parameters for which
variables were const then instantiate them by default with the
var status.  The problem is that will only work with C++11 or by
wrapping everything in a struct and functor --- C++03 doesn't allow
defaults for template parameters in function calls.

An alternative that I believe Ben (or maybe Marcus) came up with is
to call the var-based version once with propto and the double-based version
once without propto, and then calculate the difference.  Then you can
keep calling the double-based version, which should be cheaper (unless
the normalizing constant is super expensive), and just subtract the
difference.

> More specifically: my ALP.stan model file goes through the magic box and I get ALP.cpp. Within is my beautiful log prob function with log det Jacobians, etc. I can call that guy and only pay the price of evaluating the function, right? That whole process of .stan -> .cpp (or any other expensive procedure behind the scenes) is only done ONCE, correct?

Correct.  Otherwise it'd be like 10s per function call!

> Sorry for these naive questions! You guys have been super helpful.

I don't know how to make the big picture of what's going
on clearer.  Maybe sitting down with Daniel or with me once
I get back a week from Wednesday?

- Bob

messages.subject: Fwd: [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, August 2, 2014 7:12:15 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Issue One: What is Convergence?
>
> There is no hard cutoff between “transience” and “equilibrium".  What happens is that as N-> infinity the distribution of possible states in the Markov chain approaches the target distribution and _in that limit_ the expected value of the Monte Carlo estimator of _any integrable function_ converges to the true expectation.  There is nothing like warmup here because in the N->infinity limit the effects of initial state are completely washed out.
>
> The problem is what happens for finite N.  If we can prove a strong _geometric ergodicity_ property (which depends on the sampler and the target distribution) then one can show that there exists a finite time after which the chain forgets its initial state with a large probability.  This is both the autocorrelation time and the warmup time — but even if you can show it exists and is finite (which is nigh impossible) you can’t compute an actual value analytically.

If you could show analytically that a strong form of ergodicity holds in some situation, great. But in any situation (where there are multiple chains), you can make a plot like the right half of this one

 <https://lh5.googleusercontent.com/--MaPyWRghKY/U90XNbTK3hI/AAAAAAAAAYg/YxdnCTBbyMY/s1600/comparison.png>
and conclude that the post-warmup draws that Stan produces for this (hierachical overdisperssed Poisson) model are essentially independent of each other after 6 or 7 lags. So, a strong form of ergodicity presumably held whether it could be proven or not, and convergence shouldn't be a problem in this case, which is suggested by all the diagnostics including the p-value of 0.065 for a test of the null hypothesis that the (thinned, split) chains have the same distribution.

If on the other hand you look on the left at a mostly blocked Gibbs sampler for the same posterior distribution, the draws are still highly dependent after 640 lags, so a strong form of ergodicity is probably not holding and you are more in the dark (although the Rhats are all less than 1.05).

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.body_plain:
No.

No, no, no.

No, no, no, no, no, no.

The problem with Rhat is that it is _necessary_ but not _sufficient_.  The ridiculously dangerous thing about simple MCMC algorithms is that they can fail with absolutely no diagnostics.  For example, consider a Cauchy seeded in the bulk — with high probability it never reaches the tails and produces under-dispersed samples that look fine under any check.

This is essentially why Geyer was so fervently against Rhat back in the day — if you can’t guarantee that the sampler will work okay than diagnostics like Rhat will never be enough to ensure that everything is working.  There may be hope for HMC but I can’t promise anything yet — hopefully we’ll have something within the next few months if the mathematics conforms to my intuition…

Yes, we've been discussing this kind of plot on stan-dev for a while because it isn't part of Stan and generally a work in progress that isn't ready for stan-users. See

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/_SJBiCaUbt4/I_G38zlHGmoJ
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/_SJBiCaUbt4/I_G38zlHGmoJ

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/89GSQ9wrIQI/KBMKxvYYW8MJ

The first link has the code. The distance correlation is a scalar function of two vectors that is zero iff the two vectors are independent, but yes, that is done for every iteration (pooling the chains) and a few different lag lengths. I usually don't show the individual points but rather a lowess curve through the invisible points for a given lag. Then I find the lag length where the post-warmup draws become essentially independent and use that as a thinning interval for a permutation test of the null hypothesis that all the chains have the same distribution (which assumes independent draws and two finite moments).

As you can read, Mike disagrees. Andrew implicitly disagrees for the opposite reasons. Bob is pretty neutral. And no one else has made their opinion known.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
The problem is statements like "the dependence between draws is essentially zero after 5 to 7 lags, in which case a strong form of ergodicity presumably holds, in which case convergence shouldn't be a problem”.  Ultimately the issue is that when geometric ergodicity does not hold everything can look fine and there are no numerical diagnostics to indicate that something is wrong.  Just because Gibbs, Random Walk Metro, and HMC all converge to the same distribution doesn’t mean that it’s the correct equilibrium distribution — indeed when algorithms fail they tend to fail in the same way.

So we agree that Rhat is necessary but not sufficient, but we disagree that if multiple sampler agree then everything is fine.  Unless I’m misunderstanding what you’re trying to claim.

On Sunday, August 3, 2014 2:10:35 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> The problem is statements like "the dependence between draws is essentially zero after 5 to 7 lags, in which case a strong form of ergodicity presumably holds, in which case convergence shouldn't be a problem”.  Ultimately the issue is that when geometric ergodicity does not hold everything can look fine and there are no numerical diagnostics to indicate that something is wrong.

For even the weak form of ergodicity, we know that if you let that Markov chain run for an infinite number of iterations and let the lag between any two draws go to infinity, then those two draws will approach independence. In practice with n draws and m chains, we would like to see negligible dependence for all post-warmup draws that are separated by s lags. And there are plenty of examples where we see that for some manageable s and plenty of examples where we do not.

So, the question seems to be: Can the dependence seem negligible when in reality, it is non-negligible? That could happen if A) the unbiased distance correlation estimator systematically underestimated the dependence at s lags or if B) the distance correlation were zero at s lags for m chains and n iterations but would become non-zero if n or m were larger. B) can't be ruled out from the iterations that you have, but those concerns hold for any empirical diagnostic.

On A), the distance correlation requires finite first moments, so I don't know what would happen to the estimator if that condition didn't hold, but otherwise I have a hard time seeing what could go badly wrong since the estimator utilizes the m * (m - 1) / 2 distances between chains and two fixed time points (t and t - s), rather than the within-chain information that makes estimation complicated. To be on the safe side, I guess you could use the biased distance correlation estimator that overestimates when there is independence, but then you would need a much larger m.

> Just because Gibbs, Random Walk Metro, and HMC all converge to the same distribution doesn’t mean that it’s the correct equilibrium distribution — indeed when algorithms fail they tend to fail in the same way.

In this case, I was trying to show why I would be skeptical about Gibbs (with a MH step for one parameter) because there was really no reasonable lag length where the dependence became negligible. So, there was no reason to think a strong form of ergodicity held and also I couldn't test the null hypothesis that the chains all had the same distribution. The only reason I had to not be skeptical of Gibbs in this case was that yielded results that were similar to NUTS where I was optimistic about because a thin interval of s=6 appeared to yield negligible dependence and failed to reject a null that the split chains all had the same distribution. Moreover, if we go back to the first time I did one of these comparisons:

 <https://lh5.googleusercontent.com/-dDtvjUXD0FE/U98mPxqSCBI/AAAAAAAAAYw/Vs1moN-dRP0/s1600/dependence.png>
the Gibbs sampler on the right for a probit model with data augmentation is geometrically ergodic, and NUTS with a logit link is essentially the same at two or more lags. If that is what the distance correlation looks like under geometric ergodicity, then I wouldn't be surprised if you could prove that NUTS was geometrically ergodic under some conditions on the posterior distribution, because that is what the plot looks like for Stan a lot of the time, even for some hierarchical models like the one I did yesterday.

It would be good to look at these plots under conditions where the Markov chain is known to be ergodic but not geometrically ergodic, but I only know of sufficiency conditions for being geometrically ergodic.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
> For even the weak form of ergodicity, we know that if you let that Markov chain run for an infinite number of iterations and let the lag between any two draws go to infinity, then those two draws will approach independence. In practice with n draws and m chains, we would like to see negligible dependence for all post-warmup draws that are separated by s lags. And there are plenty of examples where we see that for some manageable s and plenty of examples where we do not.
>
> So, the question seems to be: Can the dependence seem negligible when in reality, it is non-negligible? That could happen if A) the unbiased distance correlation estimator systematically underestimated the dependence at s lags or if B) the distance correlation were zero at s lags for m chains and n iterations but would become non-zero if n or m were larger. B) can't be ruled out from the iterations that you have, but those concerns hold for any empirical diagnostic.
>
> On A), the distance correlation requires finite first moments, so I don't know what would happen to the estimator if that condition didn't hold, but otherwise I have a hard time seeing what could go badly wrong since the estimator utilizes the m * (m - 1) / 2 distances between chains and two fixed time points (t and t - s), rather than the within-chain information that makes estimation complicated. To be on the safe side, I guess you could use the biased distance correlation estimator that overestimates when there is independence, but then you would need a much larger m.

Your intuition here holds only for geometrically (and uniformly) ergodic chains, which is the point I keep trying to make.

The problem with sub-geometric ergodicity is that you are guaranteed unbiasedness only in the infinite limit and you have no understanding of _how_ the expectations converge to that unbiased estimate.  In particular, there are no guarantees for the accuracy and precision of finite-N estimates and no guarantee for the dependence or independence between states a finite number of transitions away from each other.  Hence any lag-based analysis is meaningless for exactly the circumstances you are trying to diagnose.

For example, a hyperparameter might get stuck and the chain ends up sampling from the distribution conditioned on the initial value of that hyperparameter.  When the hyperparameter does move it may tend to jump to other extreme values and the chain continues sampling from the new conditional distribution.  Between any jumps everything looks fine and any lag-based diagnostic is fine.  Rhat from multiple chains might be able to catch the problem but there’s no guarantee in theory, nor in practice, as we often seed the chains close to each other (-2:2 on the unconstrained space isn’t _that_ disperse).

When you have geometric ergodicity there are guarantees in how the chain converges to the target distribution and how the lags behave and linear autocorrelations become meaningful.

The big problem with MCMC is that if your target distribution doesn’t satisfy the geometric ergodicity conditions for your Markov transition then you are likely to get meaningless answers.  And nobody ever checks those conditions (which is why we have to be careful with the BUGS models).  HMC might actually be different (it looks like numerical divergences actually indicate geometric ergodicity failing) but it’ll be a while before we can nail down all the theoretical details.

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, August 4, 2014 5:11:30 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Your intuition here holds only for geometrically (and uniformly) ergodic chains, which is the point I keep trying to make.

Okay, if we are in agreement that for geometrically ergodic chains that have reached their stationary distribution, the plot of the distance correlations at various lags should look like that for a Gibbs sampler of a probit model with data augmentation, then it remains to establish what the plot would look like under various violations of those conditions. Here are my intuitions, which if they exist are based on plots of example models:

1. The posterior distribution lacks finite first moments: No clue what would happen to an estimator that assumes finite first moments, but this is not such a common case

2. One or more chains is not in the stationary distribution: The within-chain distances would tend to be smaller than the between-chain distances, in which case the estimated distance correlation tends away from zero. That is the reason when the chains work well (by other criteria) but the inits are bad, the plot of the distance correlation trends downward before leveling off, as in the inhalers example that I have shown before (now with log-scale on the horizontal axis)

 <https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-6_07Aam4EUI/U9_ZbugWtKI/AAAAAAAAAZQ/VrE8urSQEoA/s1600/inhalers.png>

Supposing that your eyes trick you, then you can test the null hypothesis that the thinned, split chains all have the same distribution. If you don't thin enough, then you tend to reject the null for the same reason. Otherwise, the test usually seems to result in the same conclusion that you would arrive at visually. So, you would need a failure to converge, a misleading plot, and a type II error to get into trouble.
3. The chains are possibly in the stationary distribution but not polynomially or geometricly ergodic: In that case, I would expect that it takes some large number of lags for the estimated distance correlation to be zero. You seem to think otherwise, which is why I asked if you knew an example where the Markov chain was known to be not geometrically ergodic.

One stark, simple, recent example where geometric ergodicity presumably does not hold is when the solutions to linear equations are parameterized with

and the proposal is rejected if any element of x is negative, then n_divergent__ is 1 for essentially every iteration. If the length of x is 3 with A = [1,1,1] and b = 1, then the sampling of x is a bit inefficient but we can verify it is uniform over the triangle; if the length of x is 20, then the sampling of x is terrible. The respective cases are suggested by the distance correlation plot for x:

 <https://lh5.googleusercontent.com/-2_XZJArAKzw/U9_82Vx8iAI/AAAAAAAAAZw/CGKF4iYtMJE/s1600/convex_polytope.png>
For the funnel, with and without reparameterization

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-V0GSGfCj9Hk/U9__XUfBBRI/AAAAAAAAAZ8/R0YKh0kATTU/s1600/funnel.png>
Sampling from the distribution of standardized regression coefficients under a uniform prior for a correlation matrix of order 10 (which only has 2 moments) with a good continuous parameterization and a bad discontinuous parameterization

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-wd3h_lVHi1o/U-AGH58KClI/AAAAAAAAAaM/cjLtkGs54os/s1600/coefficients.png>
A hierarchical Poisson model under Gibbs with a MH step and a barely legal inverse Wishart prior vs. NUTS when the covariance matrix of the unit-specific coefficients is integrated out

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-JRgFYBL7ScU/U-AKbkH_AqI/AAAAAAAAAaY/RjiewpiFbdY/s1600/hPoisson.png>
All the BUGS examples that I complained about (most of which have the gamma(.001, .001) thing that leads to stickiness) at

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/jEZvT9sOwnA/A4uCIQGsH5gJ

either reject the null hypothesis that the chains have the same distribution or I couldn't find a lag length that drove the estimated distance correlation to zero so I didn't bother testing that null, including the blocker hierarchical model where you

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/K8MRlZaBDMY/4KE5XZ18dEcJ

were less skeptical about the results than I was

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/jEZvT9sOwnA/qqEZcmmJQuwJ

I don't know of an example where a chain looks sticky by some other indicator but doesn't look sticky in the distance correlation plot, which I believe is due to the fact that the distance correlation estimator I have been using has nothing to do with the within-chain averages of the parameters. However, for what it is worth, these two papers have shown

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=8673044515426608265&hl=en&as_sdt=5,33&sciodt=1,33
http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=3454360930509805159&hl=en&as_sdt=1,33

that you can even do distance correlation stuff on sequences that are stationary and ergodic. So, one could --- in principle --- take each chain, copy it but offset it by s lags, and test a null hypothesis that the two sequences were independent. But, as you keep saying, unless the chain is geometrically or polynomially ergodic, there is no way of knowing in advance how large n would need to be for the asymptotic theory to kick in.

For exactly that reason, I haven't been doing that. Instead I use the cross-chain information at iteration t to estimate the distance correlation with time t-s. At time t, the m chains are some distance away from each other. At time t-s, the m chains were some distance away from each other. It doesn't even matter for the purpose of estimating their dependence if the Markov chains have a stationary distribution. You double-center the distance matrix at t and at t-s, multiply them together elementwise, take the elementwise mean of that, and divide by the distance standard deviations to get the distance correlation on the [0,1] interval (omitting a bias correction). That converges to whatever it converges to as m * (m - 1) / 2 gets large, (side note: the default of m = 4 is not so good because the plots are more irregular), but why would it converge to zero if the chains at time t weren't essentially independent of where they were at t - s and stay near zero until t = n? Mathematically, that could happen if the distance standard deviations in the denominator were dramatically overestimated relative to the distance covariance in the numerator, but I don't see why that would happen or furthermore if it did happen, why it doesn't happen with a lag length of 1?

In your example:

> For example, a hyperparameter might get stuck and the chain ends up sampling from the distribution conditioned on the initial value of that hyperparameter.  When the hyperparameter does move it may tend to jump to other extreme values and the chain continues sampling from the new conditional distribution.  Between any jumps everything looks fine and any lag-based diagnostic is fine.

Between jumps it doesn't look fine; it looks like the plots above when the lines start majorly ascending. Let's say the first chain is stuck at time t - s and stays stuck until time t, while the other m - 1 chains are unstuck. So, you have the matrix at time t - s

          theta_1, theta_2, ..., theta_p
Chain 1:     a       b      ...,     c
Chain 2:     d       e      ...,     f
...
Chain m:     g       h      ...,     i

and the matrix at time t

          theta_1, theta_2, ..., theta_p
Chain 1:     a       b      ...,     c
Chain 2:     j       k      ...,     l
...
Chain m:     o       q      ...,     r

So, how could the estimated distance correlation systematically come out to zero when the two are linked by the fact that Chain 1 is {a,b,...,c} in both periods?

If Chain 1 gets unstuck at time t + 1, maybe it gets essentially independent of where it was at t - s + u after u iterations. But you wouldn't see a continuous stretch of near-zero distance correlations at s lags; you would see bounces upward. These might be minor as in the 3 dimensional convex polytope case (with 1 chain getting stuck briefly around iteration 10000) or major as in all the examples above where I think the chains are doing poorly. Even if you make s larger than the longest overlapping stuck interval for all of the chains, you see the bounces for shorter lags, which is why I always start the plot with a lag length of 1. But if you increase s so that it is larger than the longest stuck interval, then either the longest stuck interval is not that long, or your thinned sample of m * n / s draws is too small to adequately test the null that the m chains have the same distribution, or you make n huge. All three of those are decent outcomes.

> The big problem with MCMC is that if your target distribution doesn’t satisfy the geometric ergodicity conditions for your Markov transition then you are likely to get meaningless answers.  And nobody ever checks those conditions (which is why we have to be careful with the BUGS models).  HMC might actually be different (it looks like numerical divergences actually indicate geometric ergodicity failing) but it’ll be a while before we can nail down all the theoretical details.

Potentially meaningless parameter averages, yes. But I am not convinced that in the case that the parameter averages are meaningless precisely because the within-chain draws are too dependent, the estimated distance correlation would somehow remain terminally zero if you rely on the between-chain information to estimate it. At least it doesn't in any of the examples above.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.body_plain:
a) Polynomial ergodicity is not good enough — geometric or uniform is required, and you don’t get uniform ergodicity on non-comptact spaces.

b) EVERYTHING is an integral and you have to treat it as such.  The appropriate question is not whether the function whose expectation you’re taking diverges or whether the measure you’re taking an expectation with respect to has finite moments, the question is whether or not the integral \int f(x) dp(x) is finite (mathily, whether f \in L^{1} \left( p \right) or not).  This has to be verified on a case-by-case basis.

To go further we have to be careful with the notation.  A Markov chain is a generated by a transition operator, T, that maps measures to measures.  We start with a delta function at the initial state, delta_{q}, and after time n get the measure delta_{q} T^{n} (T acts on the right because statisticians hate good notation).    The distribution of the Markov chain is then a semi-direct product measure,

delta_{q} T^{0} \ltimes delta_{q} T^{1} \ltimes … \ltimes delta_{q} T^{n}

The actual Markov chain is a sample from this distribution and the semi-direct product just means that if we sampled the state q_{i} then q^{i + 1} ~ delta_{q_{i}} T.

c) One of the really important properties of geometric ergodicity is that we can constrain _how_ the delta_{q} T^{i} converge to the target distribution as i \rightarrow \infty.  This allows us to ensure that correlations between different delta_{q} T^{i}, and even the variance of different samples from delta_{q} T^{i}, are well-defined.  In this case you can calculate all the lags you want and argue for stationarity.  But theoretically the time to stationarity should be approximately the same as the autocorrelation time, so if you rely on these diagnostics entirely you’re throwing away good information (comparing the time for Rhat or any distance diagnostic to converge vs autocorrelation time would be a good project).

d) Without geometric ergodicity we are boned, because we don’t even know how the intermediate distributions, delta_{q} T^{i}, relate to the asymptotic target measure.  These means that within chain and between chain expectations may be ill-defined and not close to the asymptotic values for any finite i.

I’m not advocating abandoning Rhat and other diagnostics entirely — their failure is informative.  The problem is trusting that these diagnostics are sufficient — they are not and should not be considered as such.  For example, in the case of “jumping” hyper parameters the diagnostics will catch short periods, but remember that the centered-parameterization of the 8-schools got stuck only after hundreds of thousands of iterations which is far more than anyone would run.

That said, there is still the problem of what happens to these diagnostics when the chain is geometrically ergodic but the delta_{q} T^{i} are not Gaussian (false positives are really bad here).

Also, the log scale on your plots is hugely misleading.  The variations in the retained parts are of the same time scale as all of the warmup, indicating that warmup was just nowhere near long enough.

BH package is at as far as R goes, which is currently on

just lag in all of its bug fixes.  We just don't have the people power
for the alternative, which is continuing to maintain multiple
versions and patch them all.

I'm interested and took a run at it, but it was too big a project for me
given my unfamiliarity with stan internals and Debian packaging.

For reasons described more fully below, the existence of a downstream
package, e.g., for Debian, does not necessarily mean you need to pin on
a specific library version.

The way stan is packaged as a giant collection, including most external
dependencies, was a major barrier to making a Debian package, although
the split into cmdstan, rstan, etc, which came after my efforts, may
help.  The Debian package would need to rely on the already packaged
versions of boost, eigen, the compilers, R and python in Debian.

stan itself would probably be split into several packages.  With luck
there would be a common core set of libraries (and maybe tools and
documentation) used by all the stan flavors.

stan, especially rstan, is also kind of weird in that it is itself
effectively a compiler, so that the usual model (compile the code,
package the result, and distribute it) is not quite apt for it.  Usually
there is a division into "development" and "application" packages, with
the former having stuff needed if you are developing software to use the
packaged software and the latter having what you need to run it.  Since
stan builds and compiles software in routine operations, this
distinction is difficult to apply in its case.

I'm sure packaging is possible; it's just not easy.

As for the issue of maintaining multiple versions (raised by Bob), that
could be the responsibility of the (currently non-existent!) Debian
packager rather than the core stan team.  Although it would obviously be
easier on the packagers if it were done upstream (i.e., by the stan
group), I'm not even sure that's the norm.  There are a lot of
distributions of linux--for that matter, Debian itself alway has 3,
stable (=current official release), development (=next release), and old
stable--and I doubt upstreams typically maintain all 3.  The bar is
usually pretty high (i.e., security and major bug fixes only) for
modifying a package once it's in stable, and so it's really for the
distribution (e.g., Debian) to decide exactly what code to change.

I suspect in stan a middle ground between "we will do all the packaging
for Debian" and "we will ignore packaging--someone else's problem" would
be best.  The middle ground would be making some modifications to stan,
especially the build system, to make it more manageable for downstream,
and then letting packagers to do the rest.  Such changes may be
desirable in their own right, and could facilitate things that would be
good on their own, like having a package for R that would be acceptable
on CRAN because it wasn't huge and scary.

The version in Debian stable, let alone old stable, tends to get old
quickly.  It is often not even the current version of the software at
the time Debian makes a release, because it gets frozen at some earlier
state.

2 last wrinkles: There are also backports, which are the current version
(or at least the one in Debian development branch) built to work on the
stable distribution.  Only some packages are in backports.  Only some of
those are completely current with upstream.   In some cases they can't
be; for example julia is not in stable and never will be backported
because it requires a more recent version of LLVM than is in stable.
Second, there is also Debian "experimental" for cutting edge stuff
that's ahead of the development release.

Ross Boylan

messages.body_plain:
I'm still chewing through the math you set out, but a few tangential points:

On Tuesday, August 5, 2014 4:43:49 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> a) Polynomial ergodicity is not good enough — geometric or uniform is required, and you don’t get uniform ergodicity on non-comptact spaces.

OK. I just mentioned polynomial because sometimes it implies the MCMC CLT. I don't think really good polynomial could be distinguished from geometric anyway using just the empirical draws.

> c) One of the really important properties of geometric ergodicity is that we can constrain _how_ the delta_{q} T^{i} converge to the target distribution as i \rightarrow \infty.  This allows us to ensure that correlations between different delta_{q} T^{i}, and even the variance of different samples from delta_{q} T^{i}, are well-defined.  In this case you can calculate all the lags you want and argue for stationarity.  But theoretically the time to stationarity should be approximately the same as the autocorrelation time, so if you rely on these diagnostics entirely you’re throwing away good information (comparing the time for Rhat or any distance diagnostic to converge vs autocorrelation time would be a good project).

I recognize that there is some art to judging the plot that is fallible and even if you get that right, the test of the null that the chains have the same distribution is subject to type I and type II errors, and what you would really want is to be able to reject a null hypothesis that the chains do not have the same distribution. So, you can't rely on that exclusively. But my goal was to see how far you can get with a single plot and a single test. From the literature and also my experience with social scientists, one of the big practical issues with the marginal diagnostics they are using is that if there are a moderate number of parameters, some of the marginal diagnostics look better than others, and they aren't independent of each other, and people don't really know what to conclude about whether all the chains are in the stationary distribution.

The distance correlation is a scalar function of all the parameters in the posterior distribution. And the alternative hypothesis is that at least one of the chains has a different distribution than the rest, which is pretty general compared to a more limited thing like the means of one of the chains are too different relative to the other chains.

I agree that comparing with autocorrelation time would be instructive, but I would expect it to show what

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=3454360930509805159&hl=en&as_sdt=1,33

shows when comparing distance correlation with autocorrelation with data that varies over time: namely, that distance correlation is also sensitive to nonlinear dependence and that distance correlation is sensitive to the cross-parameter dependence that we would expect to see in hierarchical models (i.e. beta at time t depends on alpha at time t - s).

> Also, the log scale on your plots is hugely misleading.  The variations in the retained parts are of the same time scale as all of the warmup, indicating that warmup was just nowhere near long enough.

>From my perspective, either it stays zero from iteration 1000 to iteration 10000 or it was never zero at any point, so having more pixels on iteration 1 to iteration 1000 when things are changing makes it easier to see the change. But I can do them on the linear scale just as easily.

Ben

C++11 would be fine, except perhaps for oldstable.

When a Debian package depends on "Boost", it really means that it depends on a sublibrary of Boost. Taken as a whole, Stan depends on a lot of Boost sublibraries, but if Stan itself (not the interfaces per se) were more separatable, each part of Stan could become a Debian package that itself depends on fewer sublibraries of Boost. So, for example, nomad would be something stand-alone that maybe depends on a little bit of Boost. And stanc depends on Spirit and some other Boost stuff but not the Boost math stuff that libstan depends on. The documentation could be a separate Debian package that depends on LaTeX but not Boost or Eigen, etc.

Ben

an installation of CmdStan [or at least core stan libraries]"?
Or have the R build procedure check for the existence of necessary tools

For example, I know that Rmpi requires you to have installed mpi before
you use it; mpi installation is not part of the process in which R
builds rmpi.

Admittedly this is not one touch.  It seems to me if you want one touch
it would be best to have something that behaves like a regular R package
with external dependencies, and then have a wrapper/tarball that
includes the R library, a bunch of other stuff, and scripts to install
it.  Or just scripts that download everything as needed.

with it.

Why would it?  I don't know what the current state of C++11 support is
on linux, but even if it's not good, it will improve.  Though if current
C++11 support is not good, I guess it would be a major barrier to
current adoption, especially if the use of new features is pervasive and
the code doesn't have versions for the old standard (either in #ifdef's
or in a separate branch).

>
> I'm not sure what you mean by breaking Stan down further.

There are 2 distinct senses of "breaking down."

One concerns the way the stan code base (interpreted broadly to include
wrappers for R, python, ...) is organized and its build process is
structured.  The main modification I was thinking of here was a change
in the build procedure, not the breakdown into repositories.

The second sense of "breakdown" concerns the Debian packaging.  In the
typical case, header files and library development files go in one
Debian binary package and executables go in a separate Debian binary
package.  There might also be a debug version of the  binary packages.
All binary packages are built from the same Debian source package, and
the breakdown of the Debian binary packages has no corresponding
breakdown in the upstream source.

The general flow is
upstream source + debian patches -> debian source package -> one or more
debian binary packages
The binary packages are the ones regular users install on their systems.
In a trivial sense there are always multiple binary packages: one for
each hardware architecture Debian supports.

If upstream sources contain material that is not freely distributable
that's usually stripped out before creating the debian source.

The debian patches always include a makefile that knows how to build the
debian packages.

different libraries in place of core Stan, it might be good to change
that.

Both R libraries and Debian packages have ways of expressing dependence
on other libraries and packages; I think R packages also have a way to
at least note dependencies on things (e.g., compilers) other than R
packages.

Maybe stanc too.

Part of the reason for this is that if there were a need to update one package (whether by us or by the Debian package maintainer) then you don't need to update everything. RStan and PyStan Debian packages are a bit of a separate issue. If there were official Stan Debian packages, then making RStan and PyStan Debian packages would be easy because they would depend on the Stan packages and basically just add the interface code. But making official Stan Debian packages is pretty involved. We could have unofficial Debian packages that basically do what the interfaces do now by each bundling all of Stan as a git submodule, but I don't think there is much benefit to unofficial packages.

> OK. I just mentioned polynomial because sometimes it implies the MCMC CLT. I don't think really good polynomial could be distinguished from geometric anyway using just the empirical draws.

Careful — it only guarantees a MCMC-CLT for a very small class of function expectations which tend to not be particularly useful in practice (strong integrability conditions, often straight-up bounded everywhere.

> I recognize that there is some art to judging the plot that is fallible and even if you get that right, the test of the null that the chains have the same distribution is subject to type I and type II errors, and what you would really want is to be able to reject a null hypothesis that the chains do not have the same distribution. So, you can't rely on that exclusively. But my goal was to see how far you can get with a single plot and a single test. From the literature and also my experience with social scientists, one of the big practical issues with the marginal diagnostics they are using is that if there are a moderate number of parameters, some of the marginal diagnostics look better than others, and they aren't independent of each other, and people don't really know what to conclude about whether all the chains are in the stationary distribution.

Firstly, the “convergence” time will depend on each marginal because it depends on the function of interest.  Because Rhat and its ilk cannot disentangle lack of stationary due to transient effects or lack of geometric ergodicity, the diagnostics will always have residual marginal-dependence.  Even a joint test will depend on which functions are used.

I maintain that one issue that is not really understanding is how sensitive the algorithms are to Gaussianity assumptions (is lp__ always failing because it’s highly skewed or because it’s more sensitive to transient effects?) which just confuses the diagnostics further.

In the end MCMC always decomposes into univariate expectations, and fundamental autocorrelation and convergence to stationarity will depend on the functions chosen, including auto and cross correlations.

> The distance correlation is a scalar function of all the parameters in the posterior distribution. And the alternative hypothesis is that at least one of the chains has a different distribution than the rest, which is pretty general compared to a more limited thing like the means of one of the chains are too different relative to the other chains.

But we can appeal to stationarity for the distribution of the expectations — we can’t for the limiting distribution itself, which means strong Gaussianity assumptions will lead to poor power estimates.

OK, back to the justification of the distance correlation stuff:

On Tuesday, August 5, 2014 4:43:49 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> b) EVERYTHING is an integral and you have to treat it as such.  The appropriate question is not whether the function whose expectation you’re taking diverges or whether the measure you’re taking an expectation with respect to has finite moments, the question is whether or not the integral \int f(x) dp(x) is finite (mathily, whether f \in L^{1} \left( p \right) or not).  This has to be verified on a case-by-case basis.
>
> To go further we have to be careful with the notation.  A Markov chain is a generated by a transition operator, T, that maps measures to measures.  We start with a delta function at the initial state, delta_{q}, and after time n get the measure delta_{q} T^{n} (T acts on the right because statisticians hate good notation).    The distribution of the Markov chain is then a semi-direct product measure,
>
> delta_{q} T^{0} \ltimes delta_{q} T^{1} \ltimes … \ltimes delta_{q} T^{n}
>
> The actual Markov chain is a sample from this distribution and the semi-direct product just means that if we sampled the state q_{i} then q^{i + 1} ~ delta_{q_{i}} T.

I'm now imagining a continuum of Markov chains in my head that have each been run to state q^{t - s}.
If we suppose that the chains are not all in the stationary distribution at t - s, then maybe the integral over the chains would be finite and maybe it wouldn't.
If we suppose that the chains are all in the stationary distribution at t - s, then in my head the integral over the chains would be the same as the integral of the posterior over the parameter space.
In practice, I would have m Markov chains that have each been run to state q^{t - s} and then further to state q^{t}
If we suppose that the m chains are not all in the stationary distribution at t - s, then what the distance covariance estimator from t - s to t is estimating is not so well-defined: At best, it would be some weird mixture and at worst, there is no there there. But as long as the distance covariance estimator is bounded away from zero as m increases, we wouldn't incorrectly conclude that the m chains at state t are independent of where they were at state t - s. Intuitively, if the chains have different distributions then successive draws from the same chain are going to tend to be closer to each other than to draws from different chains. But there may be some additional scope for theoretical trouble when you divide the estimated distance covariance by the estimated distance standard deviations to the get the estimated distance correlation on the [0,1] interval.
If we suppose that the m chains are all in the stationary distribution at t - s, then the estimated distance standard deviation at t - s and at t both converge in probability as m increases to that for the posterior distribution (if the posterior distribution has finite first moments). The distance correlation between state t - s and state t induced by applying the transition operator s times has to be less than 1 I think because if it were 1, then the two states would be related by an orthogonal rotation, which wouldn't even be a viable Markov chain. If so, then we consistently estimate it as m increases and the limit is zero iff the m chains were independent at state t of where they were at state t - s, which isn't going to literally happen but it might be only negligibly far from zero.

> d) Without geometric ergodicity we are boned, because we don’t even know how the intermediate distributions, delta_{q} T^{i}, relate to the asymptotic target measure.  These means that within chain and between chain expectations may be ill-defined and not close to the asymptotic values for any finite i.

I'm still not understanding --- for the purpose of estimating the distance correlation between two states, t - s and t --- why you are doing the asymptotics with respect to the number of iterations instead of with respect to the number of chains. (I understand why you would do the asymptotics with respect to the number of iterations for the substantive analysis and why you would be worried about the expectations if geometric ergodicity didn't hold). I could also see why if geometric ergodicity did not hold, it would be less likely that all m chains were in the stationary distribution by state t - s and thereby affect the probability that we were in situation 1) vs situation 2) above, which is what we are trying to decide between.

As I read it, it seems as if the structure of your argument is: If geometric ergodicity does not hold, then the dependence between state t - s and t may be so severe that if we input m independent realizations to the distance correlation estimator, the result may get close to zero and stay near zero for all post-warmup values of t (with s provisionally fixed), despite the theoretical property that the distance correlation is zero iff the two states are completely independent.

And I think a more plausible argument is structured as: If the dependence between state t - s and t is severe, then if we input m independent realizations to the distance correlation estimator, the result will not get close to zero and stay close to zero for all post-warmup values of t for any reasonable value of s relative to n. And that is what all the "bad chain" examples I have done so far seem to have shown.

> For example, in the case of “jumping” hyper parameters the diagnostics will catch short periods, but remember that the centered-parameterization of the 8-schools got stuck only after hundreds of thousands of iterations which is far more than anyone would run.

No empirical diagnostic could discover problems that would occur after you stop the chains, but if we look at the eight_schools example with 1000 warmup, 1000 more iterations, and m = 16 chains (again, the default of m = 4 does not seem to work well for my purposes), you get this picture, now with a bonus rug mark on the iterations where at least one of the chains had n_divergent__ != 0.

 <https://lh5.googleusercontent.com/-PJLJXDX6JyU/U-FKyEw7mtI/AAAAAAAAAa0/tTKckIGcgfo/s1600/eight_schools.png>
and I would say "This looks a lot stickier than a known-to-be geometrically ergodic chain like a Gibbs sampler of a probit model with data augmentation". But I could conceive of someone saying "This looks like the draws become essentially independent after 20 or 25 lags". At that point, the person should say "I have only 1000 retained draws, if I choose a thin interval of 25 and split the chains to do a test of the null hypothesis that all the split chains have the same distribution, I would be working with subchains of length 20, which is probably not going to provide much power." Then, that person should come to the conclusion that s = 25 is not reasonable with n = 1000, so more iterations are needed. And the more iterations you do, the worse the eight_schools model looks. But if that person instead decided to proceed blindly with the test, it would result in a rejection of the null:

> convergence(eight_schools, thin = 25, R = 199)
[1] "Multivariate loss = 1.008"
disco(x = mat, factors = chain_id, distance = FALSE, R = R)

Distance Components: index  1.00
Source                 Df   Sum Dist  Mean Dist    F-ratio    p-value
factors                31  596.90096   19.25487      1.315      0.005
Within                608 8905.04746   14.64646
Total                 639 9501.94843

So, I would say that eight_schools is another example where the distance correlation stuff would point the user in the right direction (and the marginal Rhats do not).

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.body_plain:
> I'm still not understanding --- for the purpose of estimating the distance correlation between two states, t - s and t --- why you are doing the asymptotics with respect to the number of iterations instead of with respect to the number of chains.

There is absolutely no guarantee of anything by adding more Markov chains.  None.

All more Markov chains give you is more realizations from the joint distribution over the entire chain, but you have to be very careful here because that joint distribution is not a product of distributions at each iteration but rather a semi-direct product.  For example if you run m Markov chains to iteration n you’re not drawing n independent samples from the common distribution,

\delta_{q} T^{n},

you’re drawing samples from the individual conditional distributions,

\delta_{q_{m(n-1) } T.

When you have geometric ergodicity these distributions converge in a well-defined way to the target distribution and you can start considering auto and cross correlations as well defined objects.  But without that there’s no strong information on how the \delta_{q_{m(n-1) } T are related, so calculations like the cross correlation between chains are not well-defined.

Yes running more chains tends to catch more pathologies empirically (including for Rhat), and until we understand ergodicity better there’s no reason to not run more chains if the resources are there, but there is no theoretical guarantee of anything and anything that might suggest otherwise to the users should be unwelcome.  I don’t care if it scares off users who require a single number to feel good about their analysis — great power, great responsibility, blah, blah, blah.

On Tuesday, August 5, 2014 5:45:37 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Firstly, the “convergence” time will depend on each marginal because it depends on the function of interest.  Because Rhat and its ilk cannot disentangle lack of stationary due to transient effects or lack of geometric ergodicity, the diagnostics will always have residual marginal-dependence.  Even a joint test will depend on which functions are used.

But since the distance correlation is sensitive to all forms of nonlinear and cross-parameter dependence, it is more prone to catch it for any given set of functions that the user monitors. (By default, I am including everything but for the sampling from the solution to a set of linear equations model, I restricted it to x and excluded w).

> > The distance correlation is a scalar function of all the parameters in the posterior distribution. And the alternative hypothesis is that at least one of the chains has a different distribution than the rest, which is pretty general compared to a more limited thing like the means of one of the chains are too different relative to the other chains.
>
> But we can appeal to stationarity for the distribution of the expectations — we can’t for the limiting distribution itself, which means strong Gaussianity assumptions will lead to poor power estimates.

Yes, usually the user is interested in the expectation of some function. But I think there is a lot of practical value in being more precise about when it is reasonable to say "Okay, it looks like the chains are in the stationary distribution, it looks like the adaptation went okay, now I'm just going to wait until the expectations convergence". After the waiting is over, then you don't have to look at all the stuff on the functions you don't care about substantively and can try to ascertain whether the expectations of function(s) you do care about are good enough.

But moreover, suppose that all the chains are in the stationary distribution, the estimated distance correlation at s lags is always near zero, and that really means that t - s and t are essentially independent. Then, the expectations from the unthinned sample of size m * n are converging at least as fast as they would in a simple random sample from the posterior of size m * n / s, if it were possible to draw such a simple random sample. So, we are back to the question of whether n / s is reasonably large and whether the estimated distance correlation can systematically be zero when there is non-negligible dependence between the states at t - s and t.

Ben

> disco(x = posterior, factors = data.frame(chain_id), R = R)
>
> Distance Components: index  1.00

> chain_id               31 1262.50287   40.72590      1.353      0.005

> Total                 799 24381.21432

> This is what I thought would be the main objection to my approach, that the test would too often find a statistically significant difference in distributions among the chains when there would be little damage to the substantive analysis. With NUTS and a good reparameterization, you can get it really right:
>
> mc <-
> '
> data {
>   int<lower=1> K;
>   real<lower=0> nu;                                                                           }
> parameters {
>   vector[K] z;
>   real<lower=0> u;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   vector[K] theta;
>   theta <- sqrt(nu / u) * z;
> }                                                                                             model {
>   z ~ normal(0.0,1.0);
>   u ~ chi_square(nu);
> }
> generated quantities {
>   real SS;
>   SS <- dot_self(theta);
> }
> '
>
> And you get both the marginal means and the standard deviations right plus fail to reject the null hypothesis that all the thinned split chains have the same distribution with a thin interval of just 4
>
> convergence_test(good_multi_t, thin = 4, R = 199, split = TRUE)

>

> chain_id               31  801.10788   25.84219      1.023       0.39
> Within               3968 100260.43483 25.26725
> Total                3999 101061.54271
>
> A nu of 5 is a bit on the small side for a posterior distribution with adequate data, but having 30 uncorrelated parameters in the posterior distribution would be uncharacteristically favorable.
>

I’m not quite sure but I don’t think that this scale(rank(x)) is quite working the way it’s supposed to.  For each quantity of interest, you want to rank all the simulations in all the chains.  I think that here you’re doing a separate ordering for each chain, although I can’t be sure.

Here’s some (clunky) code I wrote to do this, a few months ago:

z_score <- function (a){
  a_vec <- as.vector(a)
  z_vec <- qnorm (rank(a_vec)/(length(a_vec)+1))
  dim_a <- dim(a)
  return (if (is.null(dim_a)) z_vec else array (z_vec, dim_a))
}
rhat_ranks <- function (stan_object){
  sims <- as.array (stan_object)
  n_params <- dim(sims)[3]
  for (k in 1:n_params){
    sims[,,k] <- z_score (sims[,,k])
  }
  return (monitor (sims, warmup=0, print=FALSE)[,"Rhat"])
}

messages.body_plain:
On Aug 11, 2014, at 1:38 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> Bob, I think you're probably best suited to answer this one.
>
> I'm confused as to what stan::math::as_bool() does.

It's only used in the while loops and if loop.  It's needed
to convert var to boolean, and the behavior for non-bool
should match static_cast<bool>().

There are two fixes we need for that.

1.  correct behavior for int inputs (0 or 1)

2.  return type bool rather than int

> - For doubles, it returns a boolean true if the value is not zero, false otherwise. There's a test in there that checks that an NaN input returns true.

That's the correct behavior.  This code

  double nand = std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();

  std::cout << "nand=" << nand << std::endl;
  std::cout << "static_cast<bool>(nand)=" << static_cast<bool>(nand) << std::endl;

  if (nand)
    std::cout << "true" << std::endl;
  else
    std::cout << "false" << std::endl;

  std::cout << "1 > 4 = " << (1 > 4) << std::endl;

  std::cout << "static_cast<bool>(15) = " << static_cast<bool>(15) << std::endl;

prints out:

nand=nan
static_cast<bool>(nand)=1
true
1 > 4 = 0
static_cast<bool>(15) = 1

Now it'd be possible to have it throw, but that's not the way C++
works as is, and I was trying to follow C++ behavior as much as
possible for both ease of understanding and simplicity in coding.

Should this throw?  I can't imagine passing in nan being anything
other than an error.

> - For integers, it returns an integer that's equal to the input.

That'll work for conditionals, but it should return 0 or 1 for integers!
If you replace it with static_cast<bool>(), that's what it'll do.

> Was this an implementation of some external function? If not, are we ok with changing the spec so NaN input either returns NaN or (preferably) throws an exception? I'm a little uncomfortable with our functions swallowing NaNs.

No, there's no external version of this anywhere.

It could throw an exception if you want --- that'd be a reason for
keeping it.

Sorry I was so sloppy doing this the first time?  Can I blame
the code reviewer? :-)

- Bob

On Aug 11, 2014, at 1:58 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Ben
> I’m not quite sure but I don’t think that this scale(rank(x)) is quite working the way it’s supposed to.  For each quantity of interest, you want to rank all the simulations in all the chains.  I think that here you’re doing a separate ordering for each chain, although I can’t be sure.
>
> Here’s some (clunky) code I wrote to do this, a few months ago:
>
> z_score <- function (a){
>   a_vec <- as.vector(a)
>   z_vec <- qnorm (rank(a_vec)/(length(a_vec)+1))
>   dim_a <- dim(a)
>   return (if (is.null(dim_a)) z_vec else array (z_vec, dim_a))
> }

This kind of function is why I find R so confusing.  I can't
make heads or tails of the types, and digging into R just leaves
me more confused.

What is the type of argument expected?  I get

> z_score(c(-2,0,2))
[1] -0.6744898  0.0000000  0.6744898

which seems OK and then

> z_score(c())
numeric(0)
Warning message:
In is.na <http://is.na>(x) : is.na <http://is.na>() applied to non-(list or vector) of type 'NULL'

I cna't seem to make a 0-size array, so it looks like this function
returns a vector if the input is size 0 and an array otherwise, which
is going to be very confusing to any function using it.

I'd suggest putting your tests up first, then you don't have to hack the
+1 in length and it's much clearer what the main-line path of execution
is and what's the edge case.

What I'd like to write is this:

  z_score <- function(a) {
    if (is.null(dim(a)))
      return as.array(a, dim(a));
    a_vec <- as.vector(a);
    z_vec <- qnorm(rank(a_vec) / length(a_vec));
    return array(z_vec, dim(a));
  }

but it doesn't work because the as.array fails on c() input.
If I used

  if (is.null(dim(a))
    return a;

then we also can't guarantee the type of the return.

I have no idea why you put spaces before some function applications
or don't put a space before the {, but it seems common among our
R users.

It's not quite the same function because of the lack of +1
in the denominator, but that should be easier to explain when you write
it up, right?

> rhat_ranks <- function (stan_object){
>   sims <- as.array (stan_object)
>   n_params <- dim(sims)[3]

We should have an extractor for num_params and use that
instead of hard-coding a [3], which is just asking for trouble
in future versions of RStan.

>   for (k in 1:n_params){
>     sims[,,k] <- z_score (sims[,,k])
>   }
>   return (monitor (sims, warmup=0, print=FALSE)[,"Rhat"])
> }

Code review mode off.

- Bob

messages.subject: Fwd: rstan vs cmd stan speed
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

As suggested by Daniel, here is the threat I started:

To add to this: I think rstan could be speed up considerably if it would know about the declared data types in a model. Right now - at least from what I get from the code - is that variable names (like arrays and their indices) get assembled from the strings in the csv files. This step is somewhat time-consuming and certainly not needed if the layout of the data could be derived from the Stan model, i.e. a array of a large size is much faster processed from a statement in the model file rather than processing the individual elements from the csv.

>
> Hi Bob!
>
> Sure, we can take it to the dev list. I am not sure if writing out files with Stan and then importing is faster. At least this would require a rewrite of the read_stan_csv function (writing the csv and importing with the read_stan_csv takes longer).
>
> From my fairly naive profiling with outputs to rstan::cout I got the impression that the time rstan takes longer in comparison to cmdstan comes from a couple of places. Quite surprisingly the vector<vector> construct to save the simulated values (common/recorder/values.hpp) does not appear to be the bottleneck, i.e. I replaced that with a flat storage where I did the indexing myself, but this did not help.
>
> To properly solve the problem, this would need a bit of profiling if the Rcpp code - but here I am lost as this would require R to be build in profiling mode as well from what I read. Is it possible to run the rstan<->stan thing without R? Then one could run a gdb session on it easily.
>
> Best,
> Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: lkj cov distribution tests
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, August 11, 2014 11:14:39 AM UTC-4, Peter Li wrote:
> Are there any tests for LKJ cov? In src/test/unit/prob/distributions/multivariate/continuous/lkj_cov_test.cpp, none of the tests call lkj_cov, they call lkj_corr. I'm trying to add tests for the higher order autodiff to make sure fvars can be passed in but I don't see anything to base the tests off of.

I think we would be better off getting rid of lkj_cov because it is a combination of a lognormal prior on the standard deviations and a LKJ prior on the correlation matrix that users could just as easily do themselves with any other reasonable prior for the standard deviations. And it takes a whole correlation matrix when it would be better if the model were parameterized in terms of L. But if lkj_cov survives, then we should make sure it is tested.

Ben

rank_rhats <- function(stan_object) {
  sims <- apply(stan_object, 3, FUN = function(x) {

  dim(sims) <- dim(stan_object)
  dimnames(sims) <- dimnames(stan_object)
  monitor(sims, warmup = 0, digits_summary = 2)
}

messages.subject: stan::math::logical_and with nan input
messages.body_plain: What's the right behavior of logical_and with nan input? The spec: /** * The logical and function which returns 1 if both arguments * are unequal to zero and 0 otherwise. * Equivalent * to x1 != 0 && x2 != 0. * * @tparam T1 Type of first argument. * @tparam T2 Type of second argument. * @param x1 First argument * @param x2 Second argument * @return true if both x1 and x2 are not equal to 0. */ The behavior: stan::math::logical_and(nan, 1.0) == true stan::math::logical_and(1.0, nan) == true stan::math::logical_and(nan, nan) == true This behavior matches the spec as written, but I'm not sure if this is the right behavior. I'm guessing it doesn't have a large effect on our code, but I'd rather do the right thing since I'm looking at it. > > In R, those would all be NA. How does it consider nan to be unequal to zero? 0 == nan should be nan. That's why I asked. R's NA behavior doesn't follow the spec for IEEE's NaN. The wikipedia article on NaN has some info, but the key is that NaN is unordered: it's not equal to, less than, or greater than anything. Even itself. So NaN == NaN returns false, not NaN. I realize this is on the edge behavior of anything we can generate through the Stan modeling language, but I'd rather fix or document the behavior because we'll run into one of these functions taking in an NaN and returning a valid number and continuing, which could cause a lot of problems down the line.

messages.subject: Boost's math functions, error policies, and NaN
messages.subject_clean: Boost's math functions, error policies, and NaN
messages.body_plain:
Short: Can't use Boost's error policies to make their math library propagate NaN.

Long:
Boost's default error policy is to throw an error. For the functions where NaN input is resulting in reasonable output (like 0 or 1), this is not triggering Boost's error mechanism, so setting the policy to something else won't help.

Boost's math functions don't do error checking on inputs, so I think the reasonable thing to do is to do error checking ourselves. I guess we could test for NaN and return NaN, but if we're going through that much trouble, why not just stop with an error message that will tell us where we found the NaN?

An example of where we're running into trouble is stan::math::ibeta(a, b, x), which just calls boost::math::ibeta(a, b, x). The documentation is here:
http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_56_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/sf_beta/ibeta_function.html

The key lines are in the Description section where it states:
"All of these functions require 0 <= x <= 1.
The normalized functions ibeta <http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_56_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/sf_beta/ibeta_function.html> and ibetac <http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_56_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/sf_beta/ibeta_function.html> require a,b >= 0, and in addition that not both a and b are zero."

Since NaN doesn't follow those require statements, the function is undefined and chooses to return 0 for some cases an NaN for others. (Looks like its argument value dependent.)

Anyway, now that we know, we should be more careful going forward.

And now I see the wisdom of Bob wanting to maintain consistency.

Roughly, yes. Functions that have a double return type should return NaN at the very least. A subset of functions that have return type double will through exceptions. I think we're ok without having a hard rule as to which functions throw, but if we're relying on boost, since it'll throw on other invalid input, it makes sense to me that the function throws with NaN.

The important thing is that all Stan versions of the function behave the same way. That is, if the stan::math::foo(static_cast<double>(NaN)) throws, then stan::agrad::foo(static_cast<var>(NaN)) and the version for fvar should also throw. If bar(NaN) returns NaN for double, it should return NaN for all.

If nan input could result in a bogus calculation, then that function has to check for NaN and maybe throw exceptions or whatever. But in this case, it is just checking for NaNs inside normal_log(), in which case the worst thing that could happen is that lp__ goes NaN which is reasonable behavior. If the only thing 9% gets us is an occasional exception message that says "something is nan and must be not nan", then we have got to implement a mechanism to enable the user to turn the checking off.

If we were to switch to C++11, then there would be a standard mechanism to check whether any calculations resulted in a NaN since the last time you checked. So, if one of the proposed parameters goes NaN, then we would know not to bother with that proposal, and we wouldn't need to check for NaN inside the probability functions, unless we reserve NaN to indicate a missing value.

Ben

Great question. I might be thinking about our auto-diff incorrectly, but we don't know how many variables are involved in the expression for any of the arguments, right? Although, I guess it's only with respect to each of the variables that's coming in. Ok, I've convinced myself that we could set derivatives to NaN. I don't have a great intuition -- I'm not sure how careful our code is to handle NaN gracefully in the calculation of gradients. If we end up using Boost's math library, NaNs might get swallowed up.

So, I think what you've suggested is good:
- if a function returns NaN, set gradients to NaN.

What if we did the converse?
- if gradients are NaN, set the value to NaN. But I think this isn't going to help us identify the location of the error due to how we deal with our auto-diff. That'll be propagated in the chain method and it's already too late, right?

I don't think I have an answer that I'm comfortable with.

On Aug 14, 2014, at 11:07 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> And now I see the wisdom of Bob wanting to maintain consistency.
>
> Roughly, yes. Functions that have a double return type should return NaN at the very least. A subset of functions that have return type double will through exceptions. I think we're ok without having a hard rule as to which functions throw, but if we're relying on boost, since it'll throw on other invalid input, it makes sense to me that the function throws with NaN.

We can always wrap in a try/catch if we don't want
to throw.  That's a bit of runtime overhead, but not much.

> The important thing is that all Stan versions of the function behave the same way. That is, if the stan::math::foo(static_cast<double>(NaN)) throws, then stan::agrad::foo(static_cast<var>(NaN)) and the version for fvar should also throw. If bar(NaN) returns NaN for double, it should return NaN for all.

Agreed.  I think that's the most important consideration.

The second question is whether we want the autodiff functions
that implement std::cmath library functions to have the same
behavior as the std::cmath functions.  I was trying to do that,
but I think I failed on lgamma and some other functions that are
built in which throw exceptions when passed var arguments.

- Bob

I just have three comments. I'm a little pressed for time today and I'm not sure
I'll be able to make it for long.

1. I think it would be helpful to make the separation between model and fit
   explicit. For example, while it's convenient to pass the *fit* object to
   stan() when one wants to rerun a model, it really is the model that one is
   reusing.  Perhaps one could pass fit@model or mark the reuse of the fit
   object as a kind of convenience macro.
2. I'd like to see serialization of the fit object (and all results) separated
   from any kind of serialization of the model. Fit objects, serialized, should
   be cross-platform, whereas model instances need not be. (One should, of
   course, store a copy of the model_code, random seed, etc in the fit object.)
3. I feel like stan_optimize or stan_optimizing is clearer than stan_mle. I'd
   even prefer stan_maximize_likelihood() (well, maybe)

Best wishes,

-a

I also think (2) is critical.  I'd like to have a way to
separate out our coda-like computations from that of our
model fitting.

As to (3), once we get to naming, the hard work's done.  I think
the term "optimize" is more popular in engineering and in some branches
of machine learning, whereas "mle" is more popular in statistics.  MLE
is a pretty common abbreviation, so it doesn't bother me.  If we
choose "maximize_likelihood" --- I think we'll get a rash of typos
because it's not a common collocation, compared to "maximum_likelihood".
The problem with the latter is that it's not a verb.  The problem with
"optimize" is that it's already a built-in function in R, so just using
that causes conflicts, hence the rather suboptimal choice
of "optimizing" the first time around.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Then we can shorten maximize_posterior_density() to just map() and
be done with it.

The real question, though, is whether we want to have a single callfor
all of our sampling:

  mcmc_sample(algorithm="hmc", ... hmc config ...);
  mcmc_sample(algorithm="stretch", ... stretch config ...);

or whether we'd want to do something that calls the top-level functionality
out at the top, like

  hmc_sample(...hmc config...);
  stretch_sample(...stretch config...);
  metropolis_sample(...metrop config...);

The second issue is whether the config is one monolothic object in R
that produces a C++ config object that can be passed to Stan, as opposed
to making the config more R-like and flat.  The advantage of the latter
function calls, like hmc_sample, is that it's easier to document and test
the requirements for the config itself because there aren't so many interdepdencies
such as "parameter alpha only applies to sampler X".

- Bob

On Thursday, August 14, 2014 2:12:31 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The second issue is whether the config is one monolothic object in R
> that produces a C++ config object that can be passed to Stan, as opposed
> to making the config more R-like and flat.

That should actually be the first issue and is essentially the same question as whether the internals should be function-oriented or object-oriented? If you have an R object with methods, then you don't need to worry about name clashes or name proliferation or a bunch of other stuff

object$sample(n = 1000)

because the object knows its own configuration, including whether it is HMC or Metropolis or whatever, and knows the options for each.

If you are function-oriented, then the typical R syntax would be like optim() where you call it on a model and pass a list of configuration stuff to it

stan_sample(model, n = 1000, config = list(algorithm = "HMC"))

The former is much closer to the C++ and to PyStan. Also, you can validate objects when they are instantiated and utilize Python-style documentation conventions for the methods. The latter is what old R code has been stuck doing since the 1990s.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: Gradients of Var functions when given NaN
messages.body_plain:
Do we care about the gradients of functions as long as the result value is NaN?

In many cases, the result is NaN but the gradients are 0 or 1. For instance, if we have x*y where x is a var (with value NaN) and y is a double (that is not NaN), the value will be NaN but the gradient will be the value of y, which is not NaN. Similar issues come up in functions like fmax/fmind/fmod and a few of the operators.

I talked to Daniel about this earlier today and we're not sure what to do about this--the sample should be rejected regardless of the gradient since the value will be NaN--so we were unsure of whether the gradient mattered that much.

Just having a stan() function that inputs a path, config, and data means those little objects would have to be instantiated and if they are not returned along with the coda-like object as part of a bigger object, then they get garbage collected.

It isn't going to be much worse that it is now. As Allan pointed out, log_prob and gradient should really be methods for a stanmodel not a stanfit. But if we define log_prob and gradient methods for a stanfit that don't do anything but call the log_prob and gradient methods for a stanmodel, then we just have to change things in one place. For documentation, I think the format of R documentation for S4 classes and methods is basically worthless, so being able to document reference class methods Python-style is a lot easier for the developer and a lot more useful for the user.

Ben
