On Tuesday, August 12, 2014 1:03:17 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Yes, that makes sense.  So my point was a digression (although perhaps useful to get it out there).

Undigressing, I think the following are objectively true, if you take what I am doing and
Do the calculations on each margin, rather than the whole vector of specified quantities
Use a sensitivity parameter of 2, rather than something on (0,2) with a default of 1
Interpret the square root of the ratio of between to within as a loss function, rather than as a test statistic
Adjust the denominator with the sum of a truncated autocorrelogram, rather than thinning

then you have the Rhats calculation, and you can do it on split chains if you want. If so, then the more subjective pros and cons of those 4 changes for answering the question of whether all the chains have converged in distribution to the posterior (as opposed to the question of whether the means have converged in probability to the posterior expectations) are:
Pro: nothing that I can think of. Con: "Good" margins are insufficient to conclude the chains have converged and invites the practical problem with high-dimensional models that the margins can differ in the degree to which they are "good".
Pro: maximum power against mean differences. Con: Zero power against non-mean differences, which is proven in the paper that derives the test. I think the con vastly outweighs the pro here because I can't recall ever seeing a set of Markov chains that differ only in their means, but it is not hard to construct examples (like the t with either large dimension or small degrees of freedom) where short chains differ in their distributions but not in their means.
Pro: loss functions quantify the practical significance of not running the chains longer. Con: only interpretable as a loss function if all the chains have converged in distribution to the posterior, which is the question we are trying to answer
Pro: Doesn't throw away any draws and thus estimates autocorrelations more precisely. Con: Does not capture non-linear dependence (and combined with 1, does not capture cross-parameter dependence).

Additionally, in practice, my approach seems to require more than 4 chains, which tends to expose more problems but takes more wall time to execute. Also, for values of the sensitivity parameter less than 1, the test is valid if the posterior distribution lacks finite variances, while the Rhat is not.

Is there anything more that should be considered? If not, I would conclude that users should test the null that all the thinned, split chains have the same distribution against the alternative that at least one has a different distribution, where the thinning interval is chosen from the dependence plot as the smallest one where the estimated dependence is near zero over the entire post-warmup period. Then, if they fail to reject that null --- and do not see any problems via other plots and stuff --- then they should look only at the Rhat(s) for the function(s) of interest to decide if they are estimating the expectation(s) precisely enough. Here, it is useful to know that means from the unthinned sample are converging in probability to the posterior expectations at least as fast as they would in a hypothetical simple random sample from the posterior whose size is equal to that of the thinned sample. But that can be a vacuous statement if the thinned sample is small, so an Rhat for the margin(s) of interest would be helpful information.

Michael, I think, is mostly arguing from the other direction, that in the absence of geometric ergodicity my approach could suffer from the same problems as Rhat. Based on my experience, I don't think that is true. Specifically, the fact that there are several examples where the null is rejected when the Rhats are small and no examples that I know of (with 8+ chains) where the null is not rejected when the Rhats are not small, suggests that it does not suffer as badly as Rhat in slow convergence situations. They both have difficulty with multimodal posteriors but that is more of an issue with the samplers than the diagnostics.

Ben

messages.subject: namespace and function resolution in generated Stan programs
messages.subject_clean: namespace and function resolution in generated Stan programs
messages.body_plain:
I was talking to Daniel and Peter on Thursday about scopes
and just realized when I was making a fix over the weekend
that we generate

  using stan::math::lgamma;

and

  using stan::math;

for each Stan program.

I had taken out the first one, thinking it would be redundant
with the using stan::math, but it's not.  Without the explicit
using statement for lgamma, the result is a namespace ambiguity
between ::lgamma and stan::math::lgamma;  with the using statement,
it resolves to stan::math.

So this is how we'd override the use of the standard (std::) or top-level
(::) namespaces to use our own definitions.

- Bob

messages.subject: command-line and RStan config
messages.body_plain:
<can_of_worms>

I'm listing out some slightly finer-grained commands than Andrew
used to help illustrate what we'll need to do with config.  I didn't
want to just go crazy overwriting the Wiki

  https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/Interfaces-3.0-Spec

without discussion.

Allen hinted that PyStan can follow along with what RStan does, but
if there are PyStan-specific issues, now's the time to bring them up!

I think there are good motivations for the finer-grained functions,
namely so that we can compile a model and reuse it with different
data without recompiling.  And do all of this with log prob and
gradients without ever calling sampling or optimizing functions.

At the same time, I imagine most R users will use something like
the existing stan() function for sampling or the existing optimizing()
function for MLEs.

If we have these finer-grained functions in R, there are two issues:

1.  How do we configure them?  The lower-level functions only require
parts of the total configuration needed for stan() for sampling
and/or optimizing() for optimization with uncertainty, etc.

2.  Do we want to implement the stan() and optimizing() commands in RStan
using the lower-level RStan API pieces, or do we want to have callbacks
into a larger Stan object in C++ with the existing uber-config object.
I've been lobbying for the former.

But I don't imagine most R users would build what they needed out
of this low-level R API, but rather they'd use something like the existing
stan() or optimizing() commands.

The question is then whether we want to build RStan's higher-level ops
out of these lower-level ops or whether we want one big Stan function
implemented in Stan C++ and configured from RStan and with callbacks
for whatever functionality we need in Stan.  Then we probably would try
to create the pieces by running samplers for 0 iterations or whatever
other hacks we needed to do to make the R interface clean from the R
user perspective.

Each object could potentially hold refs to everything it was constructed
with as well as intermediate states it went through, though I'm not convinced that's
a good idea.

Note that everything here gets created in a stable state and nothing
is mutable.  And there aren't any hairball config objects.  We can be
clever on the inside with make-like behavior for the compilation and
perhaps for other objects we can re-use if they're expensive to recreate.

OBJECTS AND RELATED FUNCTIONS
=======================================

It seems like reference classes would be the way to go to create each
of the objects.

This proposal does not have the big config object like Ben was suggesting
on the Wiki.  I still don't see what that would buy us and would strongly
prefer to build modularly than with some kind of blackboard architecture.
I say again the latter is almost impossible to doc, test, and maintain
consistency for.  Everything below maintains consistency where it needs
to as well-formed objects are constructed.

RNG and States
---------------------------------------------
We need to be able to manage RNG state, which is more complex
than just a seed, at least with what we're using now.

* rng_state create_rng_state(seed);

* rng create_rng(rng_state);

* rng_state get_rng_state(rng);

Text Streams
----------------------------------------------
* textstream <- create_stream(file=path, string=value, url=url);

exactly one option must be specified;  or we could break
it out into functions (I don't see how we could overload in R).

* textstream <- create_stream_from_path(file=string);
* textstream <- create_stream_from_string(string=string);
* textstream <- create_stream_from_url(url=strings);

Structured Data Source
----------------------------------------------

* struct_data <- create_structured_data_names(names=string-vector,
                                              context=);

* struct_data <- create_structured_data_list(list=list);

* struct_data <- create_structured_data_dump_file(file = string);

* struct_data <- create_structured_data_json_file(file = string);

Compilation
----------------------------------------------
The first step is to compile the program into a shared object/DLL
which can be later populated with data.

* program <- compile(source=textstream, compile_options=...)

    compile_options includes library location, optimization level, ???

Instantiation with Data
----------------------------------------------
Populate the model with data, producing a proper density proportional
to what we want to sample with.

* density <- instantiate(program=program, data=struct_data);

The density class implements log_prob, gradients, and also
allows inspection of variable name list, constrained variable dimensions
list, and unconstrained variable sizes, as well as a translator
for constrained to unconstrained.

States and Initialization
----------------------------------------------
Create a sampler state, consisting of unconstrained values for
all parameters.

* sampler_state <- initialize(data=struct_data, density=density);

Sampler
----------------------------------------------
* sampler <- adapt_hmc(density=density, inits=sampler_state,
                       adapt_config=..., rng=rng);

The resulting sampler needs to hang onto the rng so its
state is gettable, and will also hold a density and the
current state.   Maybe this wants to be broken down into
NUTS (+/- adapted step size and mass matrix) and
HMC (+/- adapted step size and mass matrix and specified num
steps [no way to adapt num steps as is]).

Maybe we also need to be able to create a sampler without
any adaptation if we set all the params.

* sampler <- static_hmc(density=desnity, inits=state,
                        step_size=double, mass_matrix=...,
                        num_steps=int);

Also, this should probably save the intermediate steps in
case we need them for traceplotting.

And now that I write this, I see that we need a way of specifying
unit, diagonal, or dense mass matrices.

Draws
----------------------------------------------
This creates an iterator to draw a single vector of
parameter values (a sampler_state) at a time.

* sampler_state draw(sampler);

Draws a single state from the sampler and modifies sampler.  Will
the sampler state change when the sampler changes or is it a copy?

Single Chain
----------------------------------------------

Now I'm getting confused, because we probably want the chains to
be the structured, constrained values.  Or maybe not?

* chain <- create_chain(num_draws=int, num_warmup=int);

Not sure if we want num_warmup here, and num_draws
can just be to preallocate necessary vectors.

* add(states=sampler_states, warmup=boolean);

This is already not quite a sample if there are warmup iterations
involved.  Not sure if the flag is a good idea.

Where to put things like timing info?  Do we keep updating
it with a time argument on each call, or just with some
kind of final opertion that adds in a time.  I don't like the
latter as it leaves the states possibly ill defined.

The chain doesn't know anything about where it came from.

Also an issue of storage.  Do we store just something flat
and keep a reference to dimensions, or do we store with structure?
I don't even know how to do the latter in a general way in R.

Multiple Chains
----------------------------------------------
This is where we'd run all the posterior analysis and printing
from.

* chains <- create_chains(num_chains=int);

* add(chains, chain, id=int);

If we want to print times, the single chains are going to need
to have times, or the times will have to be added when the chain
is added.

MLE
----------------------------------------------
We want to create a density and what not the same way, but
I don't know that we want to put the iterator on the outside.

param_state <- optimize(density=density, init=structured_data,
                        opt_params=...?...);

I'm OK breaking this down into one function per type of
optimizer (bfgs, lbfgs, newton, conjugate gradient, etc.),
because they all take slightly different parameters.

OO Notation
===============================================
Rather than just using

  a$foo(...)$bar(...)

we can change each member function into a regular function,
and write this as:

   bar(foo(a,...), ...)

I think this may be more in line with what R users are
expecting.

</can_of_worms>

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, August 19, 2014 2:56:25 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Note that everything here gets created in a stable state and nothing
> is mutable.

I don't think having everything be immutable is the best way to go. It makes sense for some things like the compiled model wrapper or the MCMC samples. But I don't think it makes sense for something like config, where there are so many options. I think the best design would be something like

config_object <- stan_config(algorithm = "sampling", ...)

that would call a C++ function in libstan and create an R object that has the default configuration for MCMC sampling (the default would be different for optimization, etc.) that has been overwritten using the arguments passed (if any) via the ... argument. Then config_object would basically be a named list of character vectors of length two where the first element is the value and the second element is the explanation that you see in cmdstan if you ask for help. Then users could then change something like

config_object$adapt_delta[1] <- 0.6

That does mean that config_object has to get revalidated on the C++ side when the sampling starts, but that is cheap and easy. If you make the config_object immutable, then all the non-default arguments would have to get passed when it is created like

config_object <- stan_config(algorithm = "sampling", adapt_delta = 0.6)

which requires the user to know what all of the options are in advance. That doesn't make for a good interface when the Stan config is so complicated and 99.99% of things in R are mutable. A lot of progress was made with S4 objects that can revalidate themselves when one of their slots is modified but they retained the bizarre approach of defining generic functions whose signatures could involve object classes.

> OBJECTS AND RELATED FUNCTIONS
> =======================================
>
> It seems like reference classes would be the way to go to create each
> of the objects.

I agree but I think we disagree as to why. For developers, there is some advantage to making the interfaces have the same logic as the C++ (we have the model inherit from an abstract base class with methods for log_prob, gradient, etc.). But for users, the main advantage is that they don't have to read very much documentation in the Rd format. For the R user to figure out what is possible, they need to either know the exact name of the function they need to call or the name of the class that is involved in the signature of the unknown function. And those are hard to guess or remember so they have to read the documentation like a book, which is not how the documentation is organized. And a lot of users don't even read the documentation because they expect it to not be helpful and just ask questions somewhere on the internet.

Python does this much better where if you have an object called pystan, you can just press TAB after that and it will tell you all the methods that are defined for that object. And then you can get help for a particular method. In R, it would be

object$methods() # sees that log_prob is one of the methods
object$help(method = "log_prob") # in the console, sees what the arguments are / what log_prob does
object$log_prob(theta) # returns lp__ at theta

So, it is an opportunity to change the workflow of RStan users away from a function-centric approach to an object-centric approach. If we also write a lot of one-line "convenience" functions like

setMethod("log_prob", signature(object = "stanmodel"), def = function(object, theta) {
  return object$log_prob(theta)
})

then we have to document log_prob() in the Rd format, which makes users dumber.

If it is easier to maintain and test (which it probably will be), that is fine, but it would be possible to maintain and test even if doing so were difficult. If it makes it easier for R developers to build stuff by utilizing the RStan "API", that is fine. But if it is easier to document, that is a problem because the documentation is the problem that we should be trying to minimize.

> Draws
> ----------------------------------------------
> This creates an iterator to draw a single vector of
> parameter values (a sampler_state) at a time.
>
> * sampler_state draw(sampler);
>
> Draws a single state from the sampler and modifies sampler.  Will
> the sampler state change when the sampler changes or is it a copy?

sampler$draw()

would change the state and does not make a copy.

> * add(states=sampler_states, warmup=boolean);
>
> This is already not quite a sample if there are warmup iterations
> involved.  Not sure if the flag is a good idea.

I think Andrew was suggesting something equivalent to

chain$adapt(1000)

and having the opportunity to examine how things are going before doing

chain$sample(1000)

but I think that would require some changes on the C++ side.

> Where to put things like timing info?  Do we keep updating
> it with a time argument on each call, or just with some
> kind of final opertion that adds in a time.  I don't like the
> latter as it leaves the states possibly ill defined.

It may be possible to lock on the R side and permit the C++ to bypass the locks. I personally don't think it matters that much if a user sabatoges the timing output because that is not an input to anything.

> Also an issue of storage.  Do we store just something flat
> and keep a reference to dimensions, or do we store with structure?
> I don't even know how to do the latter in a general way in R.

I think the way we store stuff now is fine, which is a list of lists of vectors / matrices / arrays that is easy to convert to an array / matrix or extract a piece of.

> MLE
> ----------------------------------------------
> We want to create a density and what not the same way, but
> I don't know that we want to put the iterator on the outside.
>
> param_state <- optimize(density=density, init=structured_data,
>                         opt_params=...?...);
>
> I'm OK breaking this down into one function per type of
> optimizer (bfgs, lbfgs, newton, conjugate gradient, etc.),
> because they all take slightly different parameters.

That is five functions to document each with non-obvious names and different options where there could be one method.

config_object <- stan_config("optimizing", algorithm = "lbfgs")
config_object # sees that m is an option
config_object$m[1] <- 10

> OO Notation
> ===============================================
> Rather than just using
>
>   a$foo(...)$bar(...)
>
> we can change each member function into a regular function,
> and write this as:
>
>    bar(foo(a,...), ...)
>
> I think this may be more in line with what R users are
> expecting.

That is the problem not the solution. I guess we have to have a stan() function that can take dozens of arguments and do everything except output diagnostics. But to have a function like

setMethod("Rhat", "stanfit", def = function(object, params) object$Rhat(params))

is to avoid an opportunity to avoid shooting ourselves in the foot. It is not easy to remember if this function is called Rhat, or rhat, or R_hat, or r_hat, or R, or scale_reduction_factor, or scaleReductionFactor, or BGR, or BrooksGelmanRubin, or gelman.diag and the user has to know it happens to be called Rhat it order to lookup the fact that it takes an optional vector of parameter names. It is less hard to learn that doing

object$methods()

tells you an exhaustive list of the things that can be done with that object, including

object$Rhat(params)

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Isn’t any estimator that just uses first and second moments throwing away information?
The rank normalization is just getting the p-values right (correctly calibrating the PSRF to be
more in line with Andrew’s perspective) and not hemorrhaging more information, no?

On the other hand, I'm bit worried that rank normalisation may throw away information. Distribution of lp may have very long tail, and you've seen that Rhat for lp is often higher. Rank normalisation would transform the samples far from the tail to be more "normal" throwing away the information about that some values are extreme.

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, August 21, 2014 4:25:54 AM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> It depends on the scenario.  As with all robust methods, what we’re doing will work better in some settings (e.g., the posterior for a Cauchy-distributed quantity of interest) but not so well in others.  There’s also the issue that we currently report the posterior mean and its s.e., and these are best estimated by the moments on the original scale.  Another option would be for us to bury the posterior mean and instead lead with the posterior median and an estimate of its uncertainty.

If you want to know a PSRF for a particular margin of interest, then I think you have to use the original scale. If you are using the Rhats to decide if the chains have converged to the posterior distribution, then maybe transformations help in some cases but it is not so hard to fool it. One way is to draw from a posterior that has standard normal margins and a sufficiently evil copula density, such as the bivariate Clayton

parameters {
  real z[2];
  real<lower=0> delta;
}
model {
  real theta;
  real p[2];

  theta <- delta - 1;
  z ~ normal(0,1);
  delta ~ normal(0,1);

  p[1] <- Phi(z[1]);
  p[2] <- Phi(z[2]);

messages.subject: RStan 3 / PyStan 3 variable renaming (e.g., chains -> num_chains)
messages.subject_clean: RStan 3 / PyStan 3 variable renaming (e.g., chains -> num_chains)
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I'm working on speeding up extract() in PyStan and noticing opportunities for
making variable names more consistent between RStan/PyStan and Stan.

It would be great if the fields of a Fit object (or objects) matched the
variable names used by Stan. `chains` is the variable name in RStan and PyStan
that I think might benefit most from renaming.

For example, Stan uses `num_chains` and `num_warmup` whereas RStan (and PyStan)
use `chains` and `warmup` for storing the count of the number of chains and
warmup samples (e.g., in Rstan `fit@sim$chains`, `fit@sim$warmup`). This could
be made more consistent. Using `chains` for the count is particularly confusing
since elsewhere `chains` stores the actual data from the sampler.

Should I add this to the Wiki page? Or is there a better place for it?

This issue doesn't affect users but it does affect developers looking to wrap
Stan and looking to RStan as the "reference wrapper".

Best wishes,

-a

Alright, time to nitpick. This is what it currently looks like on the branch I'm working on.

Here are specific things questions I have. If no one has anything, I'll pick something and move on. See annotated image for numbering.
1. Should "Phi" be bold? Should "x" be italics? Should "x" match the math "x"?
2. Does anyone care that this "x" doesn't look like the other "x"? If they should match, which one should it be?
3. Order of the equations ok? I could see an argument for x < -37.5, -37.5 <= x <= 8.25, x > 8.25
4. Space between groups is 6pt. Look about right?
5. I'm using "inf" for infinity. That ok? I could use \infinity. Also, should we keep this group if it's obvious from the first group? I would think x = inf is included in x > 8.25, but I'm happy to include it for consistency.
6. I'm separating out NaN as its own group. I tried putting it within the same group as inf and it looked a little odd, but could be convinced to go that way.
7. "throws exception"? Is that clear enough? Not all functions throw; some return NaN, others return booleans or integers, so it'll probably be worth documenting behavior for each function for NaN. For the infinity cases, I could see us not explicitly stating what happens on the bounds if it's obvious. For Phi, if x = inf case isn't written out, I think it's still clear.
8. between ":" and "x" I've added a large space ("\;"). Does that look ok?

On Aug 23, 2014, at 12:05 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> Alright, time to nitpick.

Please don't encourage me.

> 1. Should "Phi" be bold?

No.  The bold part's just supposed to be like syntax highlighting
to help you scan the doc and find the definition.

> Should "x" be italics?

No, it should be in math.

> Should "x" match the math "x"?

Yes.

So that means $\mbox{Phi}(x)$ on the left.  That's using
the roman script for mathematical functions in math.

I'm also OK with $\Phi(x)$ to put it all in math notation.

> 2. Does anyone care that this "x" doesn't look like the other "x"? If they should match, which one should it be?

See above.

I'd prefer the whole thing to be math.

> 3. Order of the equations ok? I could see an argument for x < -37.5, -37.5 <= x <= 8.25, x > 8.25
> 4. Space between groups is 6pt. Look about right?
> 5. I'm using "inf" for infinity. That ok? I could use \infinity.

Yes, \infty please.  This follows from the whole thing being math.

For distributions, I was using \mbox{\sf Poisson}, which I
commonly see in books.  That's a bit different than \mbox{\tt Poisson}
or \code{Poisson}, which renders in "typewriter" code font.

> Also, should we keep this group if it's obvious from the first group? I would think x = inf is included in x > 8.25, but I'm happy to include it for consistency.

I was about to say that.  When it follows from comparisons, no
reason to include it.  I'm OK including it if we want to be
super specific -- that way the functions would match that aren't
defined with conditionals.

Are you going to define exp() the same way, with

  exp(x) = e^x  if x \in [-800,800]
         = 0    if x < -800
         = inf  if x > 800

or whatever the bound is?

This might be useful to our users to give them ideas of the scales at
which arithmetic is even remotely feasible.

> 6. I'm separating out NaN as its own group. I tried putting it within the same group as inf and it looked a little odd, but could be convinced to go that way.

I like it on its own.

> 7. "throws exception"? Is that clear enough? Not all functions throw; some return NaN, others return booleans or integers, so it'll probably be worth documenting behavior for each function for NaN. For the infinity cases, I could see us not explicitly stating what happens on the bounds if it's obvious. For Phi, if x = inf case isn't written out, I think it's still clear.

I'm ok with just "error" or "exception".  It might be even better just
to say on the outside that NaN raises an exception --- it doesn't
return the value "throw exception" as the equality sign seems to imply now
that I look at it.

> 8. between ":" and "x" I've added a large space ("\;"). Does that look ok?

I prefer \mbox{if }.  With a single trailing space.

- Bob

I think you’re trying to do too much with too few elements.  There are four key pieces that you’re trying to present:

1) The function signature
2) The function description in words
3) The mathematical definition
4) The implementation

At the very least I think you should have something like

signature (as is)
Description (as is once you remove the equation)
Mathematical definition displayed on new line
Implementation (as is)

But I disagree on the level of implementation detail.  The user shouldn’t need to know when we transition from
erf to 0 or 1, it should just work.  What is useful to the user is not the implementation but rather

1) the mathematical domain of the function
2) the practical domain of the function

(2) is the only part of the implementation that is useful to the user.  For Phi it’s all double values, but for exp
we’re limited to log(max_double) and for something like phi_inv we can quote the threshold values where
everything becomes indistinguishable from the boundary.

So, for example,

\code{ real exp(real x) }
    The natural exponential function
        exp(x) = e^{x}

    Domain: -infty < x < infty
    Range: 0 < exp(x) < infty

    Implementation Domain: -max_double < x < log(max_double)
    Range: 0 < exp(x) < max_double

Lastly, if boundary values are really considered important then we should include a plot of the function
as that will be far more informative anyways.

messages.subject: copula stuff
messages.body_plain:
I cleaned up the attached example of a copula (family of multivariate CDFs for dependent standard uniform marginals) that I posted the other day. And every continuous joint density has a unique decomposition into a copula density (evaluated at the CDFs of the margins) and the product of the marginal PDFs.

1) What is the protocol for pushing into the example-models repo? I think it should just require that the example runs, but I haven't pushed it yet.

2) We should get a grant from some finance company to implement a bunch of copula stuff in Stan.

3) Can nomad specialize in a clever way to autodifferentiate a K-dimensional CDF when there is no explicit form for the PDF? If it takes at least 2^K stack allocations, then I guess it would only be useful for small K, in which case someone has probably derived the PDF explicitly.

4) The example of a Clayton copula is useful for testing because it illustrates what can go wrong with just 3 parameters (two standard normals and a Kendall's tau). For non-zero values of the Kendall's tau, the two normals have increasing dependence in their lower tails only. Since the parameter dependence is not constant, NUTS has a non-trivial percentage of iterations where n_divergent__ != 0.

But you can manipulate the extent of the problems under NUTS with a prior on the Kendall's tau, such as a symmetric beta distribution on (-1,1) with a shape parameter alpha. If alpha = 3, then the Rhats are small whether in the original scale or in ranks. But divergence happens on about 1/3 of the iterations, so as Michael would say, you should wait for the Riemannian stuff.

For alpha <= 8, it appears that I would reject the null hypothesis that all the half-chains have the same distribution no matter how long the chains run. This is because any chain has a small probability of getting stuck briefly in the lower tail of the normals, and when that happens for some chains but not others, that is enough to reject the null. But the first two moments are right for each margin, so as Andrew would say, there would be little substantive harm if you decided that convergence had occurred.

For alpha = 8.25, 18% of the iterations diverge, and I would fail to reject the null hypothesis that all the chains have the same distribution, even with a million iterations. In other words, alpha = 8 is right near the tipping point, and as I would say, we can distinguish empirically between nonconvergence and convergence to the stationary distribution, even when geometric ergodicity does not hold.

I added an option to the pairs plot where you can split according to an arbitrary condition, rather than just putting the first few chains below the diagonal and the rest of the chains above. Here the split is according to whether tau is more than one standard deviation from zero (given that alpha = 8.25). If not, you basically have independent normals. If so, you have noticeable lower tail dependence.

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-sqxeRO2HHbE/U_o1lWj68gI/AAAAAAAAAdg/S5FO9v9aQ5w/s1600/pairs.png>
Ben

messages.subject: lm() and inconsistency of fit objects in R
messages.subject_clean: lm() and inconsistency of fit objects in R
messages.body_plain:
I looked into how lm() behaves and not surprisingly, Ben's
right --- everything's mutable.    But is that how people use it?
If so, it seems a recipe for disaster.

In particular, you can do this:

> x <- 1:10

> y <- (2 * x - 3) + rnorm(10)

> fit <- lm(y ~ x)

> fit

Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)            x
     -3.922        2.073

> fit$model <- data.frame(x=11:20,y=(10 * x - 2) + rnorm(10))

And now at this point, the coefficients stored in fit are
inconsistent with the data stored in fit.

This seems like a recipe for disaster, because if I print fit,
the coeffs don't change.  I thought I'd just be able to do
something like:

> fit2 <- lm(fit)

and have it pick up the new data in the fit object, but no luck.  I get:

  Error in if (attr(attr(data, "terms"), "response")) { :
    argument is of length zero

The doc says:

  formula : an object of class "formula" (or one that can be coerced to that class):
  a symbolic description of the model to be fitted. The details of model specification are
  given under ‘Details’.

  data : an optional data frame, list or environment (or object coercible by as.data.frame to
  a data frame) containing the variables in the model. If not found in data, the variables are
  taken from environment(formula), typically the environment from which lm is called.

I have no idea what environment(formula) does.  Is that just the top-level
environment above?  If so, the doc doesn't seem to work --- shouldn't reusing
the fit object just pick the data up from the environment?

Are there any tutorials or anything that suggest people use
lm fit objects this way, say by modifying their data (or their formula)?
Or is it just a side effect of there being no notion of const in R objects?

- Bob

On Monday, August 25, 2014 4:49:28 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I looked into how lm() behaves and not surprisingly, Ben's
> right --- everything's mutable.    But is that how people use it?

For lm() at least, that isn't how R users use it, unless they are morons.

> This seems like a recipe for disaster, because if I print fit,
> the coeffs don't change.  I thought I'd just be able to do
> something like:
>
> > fit2 <- lm(fit)
>
> and have it pick up the new data in the fit object, but no luck.

The canonical way to do this in R is to use the update() function:

fit2 <- update(fit, data = data.frame(x = 11:20, y = (10 * x - 2) + rnorm(10)))

Maybe it makes sense to have something similar for an instantiated Stan program as represented in R, that would basically just reinstantiate with new data. But it wouldn't make sense to have someone update a stanfit with new data and keep the old MCMC draws. That is why I think we should be selective in what we lock, but part of the reason why R users are so accustomed to everything being mutable is because it was impossible to make things unmutable before reference classes, which are only slowly becoming more prominent.

Ben

On Monday, August 25, 2014 5:43:36 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I wouldn't blame the users.  The doc and API seem to encourage it.
> Though it wasn't clear to me from the doc what the behavior would be
> because I didn't understand how (or more importantly why) the environment
> from the formula got involved.

I would blame the users because the users are supposed to know that the update() function is what they are supposed to use in situations like this. What I would blame R for is this: How are you supposed to know that update() is the name of the function you are looking for unless someone who knows tells you? You have to somehow land on the manpage for update, in which case you can see from the example that it works with an object of "S3" class "lm" (among other S3 classes). There is no way of looking at an instance of "S3" class "lm" and ascertaining that there is an update() method defined for it. That is what the reference classes finally get right.

> > The canonical way to do this in R is to use the update() function:
> >
> > fit2 <- update(fit, data = data.frame(x = 11:20, y = (10 * x - 2) + rnorm(10)))
>
> But this would be equal to
>
> fit2 <- update(fit$formula, ...)
>
> Why pass in the whole fit object?

Because update() needs an object of class "lm" in order to know what functionality to execute. If fit had an element named formula (which it doesn't, but maybe you meant fit$call$formula), then it would call the update method defined for class "formula", which doesn't exist, so it would fall back to the default method for the update() function, which would throw an error. It other words, neither update() nor any other R function can recognize that fit$call$formula came from fit.

> > Maybe it makes sense to have something similar for an instantiated Stan program as represented in R, that would basically just reinstantiate with new data. But it wouldn't make sense to have someone update a stanfit with new data and keep the old MCMC draws.
>
> Whew --- I thought that's what you were suggesting for this
> big Stan object.

Composite objects could be locked I think, but the question is how many read-only methods to define for them. So, I can see why it makes sense logically to define a log_prob method for the instantiated model object. But having

stanfit$log_prob(theta)

throw an error is annoying, while

stanfit$stanmodel()$log_prob(theta)

is verbose and tedious, while

setMethod("log_prob", signature = "stanfit", def = function(object, theta) {
  object$stanmodel()$log_prob(theta)
})

means that we have to document it in the evil Rd format and thus typing

posterior$methods()

wouldn't show the user that there is a log_prob method defined for the stanfit class that merely calls the log_prob method of the stanmodel class that it contains an instance of.

Conversely, I think that

config <- stan_config("sampling")

should be mutable and get revalidated when the sampling actually starts. But if the user did

posterior <- stan(..., config = config)

then subsequently changing the config object shouldn't and wouldn't cause posterior to change its draws.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Aug 25, 2014 at 1:49 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I looked into how lm() behaves and not surprisingly, Ben's
> right --- everything's mutable.    But is that how people use it?
> If so, it seems a recipe for disaster.

Everything's mutable, but users should just access elements with [[ or $ and not set them, unless they really know what they are doing.

Really, all of R's S3 OO system is based on convention and nothing is enforced. An object is only recognized as a certain class based on the value of its "class" attribute. There are no formal guarantees as to what that object contains.  E.g. this is valid code that creates an object of class "lm" even though the object doesn't have anything resembling the output from the lm function

> foo <- structure(1, class = "lm")
> class(foo)
[1] "lm"
> str(foo)
Class 'lm'  num 1
> print(foo)
Error: $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors

messages.subject: Nomad I/O Validation
messages.body_plain:
I have a little bit of time to play around with I/O validation in Nomad,
and I want to do it pretty differently than what is currently in Stan.
In particular, all of this business with propagating NaNs is bad news,
not to mention a giant rabbit whole of numerical implementation details.

My strategy moving forward is to throw exceptions, immediately terminating
the construction of the execution graph as soon as an ill-formed value is
encountered.  This will not guarantee that all the partials are well-formed,
nor that all of the dual numbers are well-formed,  but I am okay with that.

This leaves a few questions.

1)  What is validated?

We can certainly check for NaNs and domain errors.  But what about poles
like inv(0)?  Formally we could define poles as domain errors, or we could
just ignore them and let the subsequent NaNs get caught further downstream.

2) How many exceptions?

Do we have special domain and NaN exceptions, or just one common Nomad exception
with an informative message?

3) Validate inputs, outputs, or both?

We can validate input values for NaNs and appropriate domain and assume
that the output will consequently be valid.

We can also assume proper input values and assume that improper inputs
manifest as a NaN and just validate the output of the function.

Or we could validate inputs and then add an output check.  This makes tracing
errors more accurate but also requires the performance hit of checking twice
plus the developer hit of coding up two checks (although this can possibly
be mitigated with some clever wrapping).

There’s always the issue of performance.  We can enable_if gratuitously, but
there’s always the problem of the if blocking inline optimizations.  I think the
functions are big enough this point where that won’t be an issue, but it’s
something we should monitor.  We can also add an error policy to turn the
checks off, although it’s not clear if the compilers are good enough to use
that to re-enable aggressive inlining or not.

On Aug 26, 2014, at 12:16 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I have a little bit of time to play around with I/O validation in Nomad,
> and I want to do it pretty differently than what is currently in Stan.
> In particular, all of this business with propagating NaNs is bad news,
> not to mention a giant rabbit whole of numerical implementation details.

It's not just Stan.  If you evaluate exp(NaN) in C++, you get NaN,
not an exception.  Ditto 0.0/0.0.  (I don't know what 0/0 gives you
since it returns an int and there are no NaN values for ints.)

If you have exp(NaN) throw exceptions, you'll get different behaviors
with double and autodiff objects.

> My strategy moving forward is to throw exceptions, immediately terminating
> the construction of the execution graph as soon as an ill-formed value is
> encountered.

Some people and companies (e.g., Google) have a strict
no-exceptions policy in code and libraries they use.

> This will not guarantee that all the partials are well-formed,
> nor that all of the dual numbers are well-formed,  but I am okay with that.
>
> This leaves a few questions.
>
> 1)  What is validated?
>
> We can certainly check for NaNs and domain errors.  But what about poles
> like inv(0)?  Formally we could define poles as domain errors, or we could
> just ignore them and let the subsequent NaNs get caught further downstream.

There are separate errors for this kind of thing in Boost.  And even
base C++ has a few different kinds of exceptions.   You
can start defining your own exception hierarchy.  I only see that this
makes sense if there's conceivably something on the outside that can
invoke different recovery strategies under different types of exception.
I suppose you could argue that different types of error messages might
be keyed off different types of exceptions, too.

> 2) How many exceptions?
>
> Do we have special domain and NaN exceptions, or just one common Nomad exception
> with an informative message?

See above.

> 3) Validate inputs, outputs, or both?
>
> We can validate input values for NaNs and appropriate domain and assume
> that the output will consequently be valid.

What's a valid input if not one for which a value other than NaN arises?

And what about overflows and underflows?  For example, exp(1000)
overflows to +infinity, and exp(-1000) underflows to 0.  Do you want
to just return 0 and a gradient of 0?  Or raise an error?

> We can also assume proper input values and assume that improper inputs
> manifest as a NaN and just validate the output of the function.
>
> Or we could validate inputs and then add an output check.  This makes tracing
> errors more accurate but also requires the performance hit of checking twice
> plus the developer hit of coding up two checks (although this can possibly
> be mitigated with some clever wrapping).

Of course, for some operations, like factoring a matrix, there's
no way to validate the input is valid without running the function.

> There's always the issue of performance.  We can enable_if gratuitously, but
> there's always the problem of the if blocking inline optimizations.

I don't see how enable_if helps here.  If you use some kind of
branch-on-template (like we do with traits to eliminate constant terms),
then it should get compiled away.

> I think the
> functions are big enough this point where that won't be an issue, but it's
> something we should monitor.

You might want to sprinkle them with unlikely, too --- branch mispredictions
cause a big slowdown.

>  We can also add an error policy to turn the
> checks off, although it's not clear if the compilers are good enough to use
> that to re-enable aggressive inlining or not.

Yes, they are.

- Bob

> If you have exp(NaN) throw exceptions, you'll get different behaviors
> with double and autodiff objects.

Yes, we will.  And I’m fine by that.

I don’t want to deal with the abstract minutia off ill-defined specs only to
throw an error after the expression graph has been built.  We might as
well err as soon as a problem arises.

> Some people and companies (e.g., Google) have a strict
> no-exceptions policy in code and libraries they use.

Yup.  I also don’t know of any other way to handle this kind of run-time
error without worrying about the propagation of NaNs.  Also, no way
of identifying where the expression graph went sour.

> I suppose you could argue that different types of error messages might
> be keyed off different types of exceptions, too.

That is the motivation.

> What's a valid input if not one for which a value other than NaN arises?

Within the domain of the function.

> And what about overflows and underflows?  For example, exp(1000)
> overflows to +infinity, and exp(-1000) underflows to 0.  Do you want
> to just return 0 and a gradient of 0?  Or raise an error?

0 + 0.  I don’t find underflow to be a particularly worrisome error until
someone tries to invert, in which case I’d argue it’s more naturally a
domain error of the inversion.

> Of course, for some operations, like factoring a matrix, there's
> no way to validate the input is valid without running the function.

Not entirely true — in some cases you can check validity faster
than performing the decomposition.  But in any case the focus
is on scalar functions here.

> I don't see how enable_if helps here.  If you use some kind of
> branch-on-template (like we do with traits to eliminate constant terms),
> then it should get compiled away.

Ugh, I meant builtin-expect.  Again, the big issue is whether or not
the addition of a check, even with builtin-expect, will prevent the
compiler from inlining a bunch of code and causing noticeable
slowdowns.  This was a big issue with the stack expansion
checks.  I think the functions are big enough that they’re
not being inlined anywhere, but it’s hard to know a priori.

Biggest question is still unanswered — validate inputs only (requires
very strict checks and worry about things like overflow) or just have
the inputs validated for NaNs and domain errors and check again
for any divergences in the outputs?

> throw an error after the expression graph has been built.  We might as
> well err as soon as a problem arises.

The C++ spec for exp isn't ill defined!  It's clearly defined to
return NaN on NaN input.

The main problem in not following the spec is that it means people
can have code that runs with doubles and produces reasonable outputs
but can't run with Nomad.  For instance, it might execute two
statements and if statement a produces NaN use statement b.  This is
fine and fine for auto-diff, just not an optimal way to code things.

>> Some people and companies (e.g., Google) have a strict
>> no-exceptions policy in code and libraries they use.
>
> Yup.  I also don't know of any other way to handle this kind of run-time
> error without worrying about the propagation of NaNs.  Also, no way
> of identifying where the expression graph went sour.

I agree.  We originally went down the route in Stan of having everything
use Boost's traits for errors, so that we could get either behavior (return
NaN or raise exception) depending on situation.  Finally we decided to
drop potential users of the library and specialize to just exceptions.
I'm still of two minds about all this.  It's just so damn complex with the
traits-based error handling, especially before C++11.

>> I suppose you could argue that different types of error messages might
>> be keyed off different types of exceptions, too.
>
> That is the motivation.

Usually the what() message indicates what the exception is.

>> What's a valid input if not one for which a value other than NaN arises?
>
> Within the domain of the function.

I see --- this is the same beef as with the doc Daniel's suggesting.

There are two domains in play.  For exp(x), the mathematical function
is defined for x in (-inf, inf) and the output is in (0,inf).   The
floating-point implementation is defined for all the floating point
numbers, including NaN and +/- inf.  For +inf it returns +inf,
for -inf it returns 0 and for NaN it returns NaN.  Furthermore, for
values outside of roughly (-800,800) it also returns NaN.

>> And what about overflows and underflows?  For example, exp(1000)
>> overflows to +infinity, and exp(-1000) underflows to 0.  Do you want
>> to just return 0 and a gradient of 0?  Or raise an error?
>
> 0 + 0.  I don't find underflow to be a particularly worrisome error until
> someone tries to invert, in which case I'd argue it's more naturally a
> domain error of the inversion.

What's inversion?   You mean log?   Underflow's a problem if people naively
multiply a bunch of probabilities together.  There's no relevant inversion
anywhere.

>> Of course, for some operations, like factoring a matrix, there's
>> no way to validate the input is valid without running the function.
>

> Not entirely true -- in some cases you can check validity faster

> than performing the decomposition.  But in any case the focus
> is on scalar functions here.

OK.  But in some cases you can't.  Or even if you could do it faster,
you don't want to do the fast thing to check, then call the function that
has the check built in.

>> I don't see how enable_if helps here.  If you use some kind of
>> branch-on-template (like we do with traits to eliminate constant terms),
>> then it should get compiled away.
>
> Ugh, I meant builtin-expect.  Again, the big issue is whether or not
> the addition of a check, even with builtin-expect, will prevent the
> compiler from inlining a bunch of code and causing noticeable
> slowdowns.

That I don't know the answer to.  Most likely it would block inlining
and more importantly locality of code, because code still needs to
be generated for both branches, just in different orders.

> This was a big issue with the stack expansion
> checks.  I think the functions are big enough that they're
> not being inlined anywhere, but it's hard to know a priori.

If you check (x + y) for x or y being NaN, that's a pretty big
hit relative to the evaluation cost.

> Biggest question is still unanswered -- validate inputs only (requires

> very strict checks and worry about things like overflow) or just have
> the inputs validated for NaNs and domain errors and check again
> for any divergences in the outputs?

I'd say check up front when you can and when it's not too computationally
expensive.  That gives you finer granularity on reporting what went wrong.
But if it's too expensive, then it's probably not worth the finer grain
of reporting.

- Bob

the respective stacks).

> What's inversion?   You mean log?   Underflow's a problem if people naively
> multiply a bunch of probabilities together.  There's no relevant inversion
> anywhere.

A probability density smaller than the smallest floating point number being represented
by zero is fine.  You only run into issues when you need a nonzero probability density, like
trying to compute the log density...

> If you check (x + y) for x or y being NaN, that's a pretty big
> hit relative to the evaluation cost.

> But if it's too expensive, then it's probably not worth the finer grain

But we’re not just computing x + y — we’re also creating a node in the expression graph
and incrementing the stacks (which have if statements that already mess up aggressive
inlining).  All of the autodiff overhead would nominally make the check overhead
negligible.

I’m also not going to implement bespoke checks for every function separately.  That’s
too much of a pain for development and testing.  If we want a robust, readily debuggable
stack then we’re going to have to take the performance hit.

Certainly no one is monitoring Stan’s performance as these kinds of checks are
being added.

> But the spec is defined on a function-by-function basis.  That's what I mean.
>

The core C++ library functions all do the same thing.  They
all return NaN when given NaN inputs.  And they raise error
flags.  For instance, if exp() overflows, it sets errno to
ERANGE, indicating a range problem (i.e., value can't be
represented in floating point).

>> The main problem in not following the spec is that it means people
>> can have code that runs with doubles and produces reasonable outputs
>> but can't run with Nomad.  For instance, it might execute two
>> statements and if statement a produces NaN use statement b.  This is
>> fine and fine for auto-diff, just not an optimal way to code things.
>

> No it's not -- it's a discontinuous function waiting to happen.  Again, I'm

> happy making Nomad more strict to ensure that it's also more robust.

Two different kinds of robustness.  Robustness to bad derivatives
vs. robustness to bad code.  Both sides have something to say for them,
and I'm OK either way.

>
>> I see --- this is the same beef as with the doc Daniel's suggesting.
>>
>> There are two domains in play.  For exp(x), the mathematical function
>> is defined for x in (-inf, inf) and the output is in (0,inf).   The
>> floating-point implementation is defined for all the floating point
>> numbers, including NaN and +/- inf.  For +inf it returns +inf,
>> for -inf it returns 0 and for NaN it returns NaN.  Furthermore, for
>> values outside of roughly (-800,800) it also returns NaN.
>
> Checking the "empirical" domain would be a pain in the ass and cause
> no end of developer problems.  Hence the option to add an output check
> (or more precisely, checks when trying to push values and partials onto
> the respective stacks).

Agreed.

>> What's inversion?   You mean log?   Underflow's a problem if people naively
>> multiply a bunch of probabilities together.  There's no relevant inversion
>> anywhere.
>
> A probability density smaller than the smallest floating point number being represented
> by zero is fine.  You only run into issues when you need a nonzero probability density, like
> trying to compute the log density...
>
>> If you check (x + y) for x or y being NaN, that's a pretty big
>> hit relative to the evaluation cost.
>>
>>> Biggest question is still unanswered -- validate inputs only (requires
>>> very strict checks and worry about things like overflow) or just have
>>> the inputs validated for NaNs and domain errors and check again
>>> for any divergences in the outputs?
>>
>> I'd say check up front when you can and when it's not too computationally
>> expensive.  That gives you finer granularity on reporting what went wrong.
>> But if it's too expensive, then it's probably not worth the finer grain
>> of reporting.
>

> But we're not just computing x + y -- we're also creating a node in the expression graph

> and incrementing the stacks (which have if statements that already mess up aggressive
> inlining).  All of the autodiff overhead would nominally make the check overhead
> negligible.

Maybe.  Only way you'll know is to profile it.

Are if statements particularly bad for inlining?  I was thinking
of them as more problematic for prefetching instructions and
branch prediction.

> I'm also not going to implement bespoke checks for every function separately.  That's
> too much of a pain for development and testing.  If we want a robust, readily debuggable
> stack then we're going to have to take the performance hit.

How are you going to do that?  Just check the nodes getting created
on the autodiff stack?  Will you be able to have messages saying which
function the error came from?

> Certainly no one is monitoring Stan's performance as these kinds of checks are
> being added.

You're right.  But we should be monitoring this kind of thing,
at least with microbenchmarks.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
At some point, our code diverged from being compatible with
Eigen debugging.  The develop branch only passes tests
if -DEIGEN_NO_DEBUG is part of CFLAGS.

Can someone explain why this restriction got added to the code?  I'd
like to make sure it's absolutely necessary.  I don't think we have the
resources to maintain two versions of the code, but I hate to cut
off the option of running with range checks.

The specific problem I'm having is that it's very very useful for
debugging to run without disabling Eigen's debugging.

Daniel and I have started to fix these issues on:

  bugfix/issue-904-eigen-assert-bugs

The LDLT test code indicated it wouldn't run otherwise.

append_row and append_col had broken tests with mismatches sizes
which must have only run by overwriting memory without segfaulting,
but there's no indication of why.  I ifdefed out the test.

There are lots of these cases, but some of them may be dependent
on others.

I'd like to fix all of these and where it's not possible, indicate
why in the function and make sure the test code has an #ifdef so
I can run tests without disabling the debug flag.

- Bob

and autodiffed through for HMC.

could do it now.  Otherwise, we're going to have to wait
until the 2nd order autodiff is completed.  It's held up

On Aug 25, 2014, at 3:33 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Monday, August 25, 2014 1:05:24 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > 3) Can nomad specialize in a clever way to autodifferentiate a K-dimensional CDF when there is no explicit form for the PDF? If it takes at least 2^K stack allocations, then I guess it would only be useful for small K, in which case someone has probably derived the PDF explicitly.
>
> I didn't understand the question.  You mean autodifferentiate an
> iterative algorithm to compute the CDF?  Michael's leery of this working
> in general, but we found it works well enough for sampling in many cases
> (like differentiating the integrator in the ode solver).
>
> It is kind of like the ODE thing but going the other way. In the case of a copula, we know the explicit form of the multivariate CDF of the marginal uniforms
>
> F(u_1, u_2, ..., u_d | theta)
>
> but for Stan's purposes we need the (logarithm of the) copula density function, which is
>
> dF(u_1, u_2, ..., u_d | theta)
> ------------------------------ = f(u_1, u_2, ..., u_d | theta)
> du_1,du_2,...,du_d
>
>
> but for large d, there is sometimes no explicit form of f(u_1, u_2, ..., u_d | theta). So, loosely speaking, it would be great if we could evaluate
>
> var f_log(var_vector u, var theta) {
>   const int d = u.rows();
>   var p = F(u, theta);
>   var dp_du_1 = get_partial(p, u[1]);
>   var dp_du_1_du_2 = get_partial(dp_du_1, u[2]);
>   /* more of these */
>   var log_density = log(get_partial(dp_du_*, u[d]);
>   return log_density;
> }
>
> and then be able to differentiate that with respect to theta and whatever other unknowns there are to do HMC. But the above "implementation" would only work for fixed d unless there is some metaprogramming magic, and even then it would stack overflow for large d if we had to reserve 2^d spaces on the stack. So, I don't know if there is some way of specializing the var class in nomad to do that in a space-efficient way.

> Ben

> that would call a C++ function in libstan and create an R object that has the default configuration for MCMC sampling (the default would be different for optimization, etc.) that has been overwritten using the arguments passed (if any) via the ... argument. Then config_object would basically be a named list of character vectors of length two where the first element is the value and the second element is the explanation that you see in cmdstan if you ask for help. Then users could then change something like
>
> config_object$adapt_delta[1] <- 0.6
>
> That does mean that config_object has to get revalidated on the C++ side when the sampling starts,

I think it's better to validate early and often.  But then
you might not be able to do that if there are dependencies among
the config pieces.

And then you get into problems like you get with lm() in R when
the fit object can be out of synch.  If you do a fit, then change
the data in the fit object, you have what I consider to be an inconsistent
fit object.

> but that is cheap and easy. If you make the config_object immutable, then all the non-default arguments would have to get passed when it is created like
>
> config_object <- stan_config(algorithm = "sampling", adapt_delta = 0.6)
>
> which requires the user to know what all of the options are in advance.

They had to know them sometime and have them somewhere.

It's not the immutability that's key but the keeping everything in
a consistent state.

You could do something like this

  config_object <- modify_config(config, algorithm = "optimizing", tol_param=1e-6);

that would create a new object based on the existing one with changes
as indicated.  Then at least the changes could be validated all at once.
Whereas if you do this:

   config$algorithm = "optimizing"

you're left in an inconsistent state with the other parameter settings.

> That doesn't make for a good interface when the Stan config is so complicated and 99.99% of things in R are mutable.

Really?  No wonder I have such a hard time understanding it.
It seems that this is going to lead to a world of trouble with
consistency.  As in lm().

> A lot of progress was made with S4 objects that can revalidate themselves when one of their slots is modified but they retained the bizarre approach of defining generic functions whose signatures could involve object classes.

I think this would be a big improvement.  But coding those
updates is complicated as is documenting them and understanding
them from a user point of view, which is why I'd rather avoid it.

I do not like the lm approach of letting you get things in a
consistent state.

> OBJECTS AND RELATED FUNCTIONS
> =======================================
>
> It seems like reference classes would be the way to go to create each
> of the objects.
>
> I agree but I think we disagree as to why. For developers, there is some advantage to making the interfaces have the same logic as the C++ (we have the model inherit from an abstract base class with methods for log_prob, gradient, etc.).

I just meant that having objects consist of references to components
seems like the right way to go rather than copying everything.
But I probably misunderstood how things used to go.

> But for users, the main advantage is that they don't have to read very much documentation in the Rd format. For the R user to figure out what is possible, they need to either know the exact name of the function they need to call or the name of the class that is involved in the signature of the unknown function. And those are hard to guess or remember so they have to read the documentation like a book, which is not how the documentation is organized. And a lot of users don't even read the documentation because they expect it to not be helpful and just ask questions somewhere on the internet.

I'm happy with anything that improves the doc R format.

> Python does this much better where if you have an object called pystan, you can just press TAB after that and it will tell you all the methods that are defined for that object.

I think you get some of this in RStudio and in the R GUI.

> And then you can get help for a particular method. In R, it would be
>
> object$methods() # sees that log_prob is one of the methods
> object$help(method = "log_prob") # in the console, sees what the arguments are / what log_prob does
> object$log_prob(theta) # returns lp__ at theta
>
> So, it is an opportunity to change the workflow of RStan users away from a function-centric approach to an object-centric approach.

Isn't most of R function-centric if we're talking about what's
idiomatic?

> If we also write a lot of one-line "convenience" functions like
>
> setMethod("log_prob", signature(object = "stanmodel"), def = function(object, theta) {
>   return object$log_prob(theta)
> })
>
> then we have to document log_prob() in the Rd format, which makes users dumber.

I'm not sure the built-in doc is what's most important.  When I
try to use ggplot2, for example, I can't make heads or tails of
any of the built-in doc and need to go online or look in the book
for examples.

> If it is easier to maintain and test (which it probably will be), that is fine, but it would be possible to maintain and test even if doing so were difficult. If it makes it easier for R developers to build stuff by utilizing the RStan "API", that is fine. But if it is easier to document, that is a problem because the documentation is the problem that we should be trying to minimize.

My goal is for the API to be easy to write good doc for.
And by good doc, I mean easy for users to understand and
then employ.

> Draws
> ----------------------------------------------
> This creates an iterator to draw a single vector of
> parameter values (a sampler_state) at a time.
>
> * sampler_state draw(sampler);
>
> Draws a single state from the sampler and modifies sampler.  Will
> the sampler state change when the sampler changes or is it a copy?
>
> sampler$draw()
>
> would change the state and does not make a copy.
>
> * add(states=sampler_states, warmup=boolean);
>
> This is already not quite a sample if there are warmup iterations
> involved.  Not sure if the flag is a good idea.
>
> I think Andrew was suggesting something equivalent to
>
> chain$adapt(1000)
>
> and having the opportunity to examine how things are going before doing
>
> chain$sample(1000)
>
> but I think that would require some changes on the C++ side.

The current command functions on the C++ side are too monolothic.  We
can call stan with adaptation iterations but no sampling iterations, but
then there's no way to get that state back in to start again from.
We do want to add that functionality.

This is part of breaking the design down into smaller parts.

> Where to put things like timing info?  Do we keep updating
> it with a time argument on each call, or just with some
> kind of final opertion that adds in a time.  I don't like the
> latter as it leaves the states possibly ill defined.
>
> It may be possible to lock on the R side and permit the C++ to bypass the locks. I personally don't think it matters that much if a user sabatoges the timing output because that is not an input to anything.

If we want users to use it to measure how well optimized
their code is, it's going to matter.

I'd rather not have to get into locking.

> Also an issue of storage.  Do we store just something flat
> and keep a reference to dimensions, or do we store with structure?
> I don't even know how to do the latter in a general way in R.
>
> I think the way we store stuff now is fine, which is a list of lists of vectors / matrices / arrays that is easy to convert to an array / matrix or extract a piece of.

Isn't this where part of the slowdown is in the output?

> MLE
> ----------------------------------------------
> We want to create a density and what not the same way, but
> I don't know that we want to put the iterator on the outside.
>
> param_state <- optimize(density=density, init=structured_data,
>                         opt_params=...?...);
>
> I'm OK breaking this down into one function per type of
> optimizer (bfgs, lbfgs, newton, conjugate gradient, etc.),
> because they all take slightly different parameters.
>
> That is five functions to document each with non-obvious names and different options where there could be one method.
>
> config_object <- stan_config("optimizing", algorithm = "lbfgs")
> config_object # sees that m is an option
> config_object$m[1] <- 10

I prefer the modularity.  But I see the point about non-obvious names.
This is the problem I have with ggplot2.

> OO Notation
> ===============================================
> Rather than just using
>
>   a$foo(...)$bar(...)
>
> we can change each member function into a regular function,
> and write this as:
>
>    bar(foo(a,...), ...)
>
> I think this may be more in line with what R users are
> expecting.
>
> That is the problem not the solution. I guess we have to have a stan() function that can take dozens of arguments and do everything except output diagnostics. But to have a function like
>
> setMethod("Rhat", "stanfit", def = function(object, params) object$Rhat(params))
>
> is to avoid an opportunity to avoid shooting ourselves in the foot.

I agree, but I thought Andrew didn't like the $ notation and wanted
something more "standard" in R.

> It is not easy to remember if this function is called Rhat, or rhat, or R_hat, or r_hat, or R, or scale_reduction_factor, or scaleReductionFactor, or BGR, or BrooksGelmanRubin, or gelman.diag and the user has to know it happens to be called Rhat it order to lookup the fact that it takes an optional vector of parameter names. It is less hard to learn that doing
>
> object$methods()
>
> tells you an exhaustive list of the things that can be done with that object, including
>
> object$Rhat(params)

Agreed.

One issue to keep in mind is that if there's one object, this is no
more helpful than just sending the user to the index.  It's a huge
list to look through.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Nomad I/O Validation
messages.body_plain:
Okay, let me step back a second.  What is the point of input/output validation?

C++ handles domain errors by outputting a NaN and letting that propagate through the expression graph.
This would be by far the simplest and most computationally efficient strategy, with our checking the
output value at the end to see if the results are valid.

Stan currently has exceptions for domain errors (at least the probability distributions do).  This makes it
easy to identify where a problem occurs.  Checking for NaNs at input and at output and throwing exceptions
also helps with identifying problems.  The issue with all of these checks and throws is that the code
becomes a lot uglier and significantly slower.  Adding template parameters to turn off the checks makes
the code even uglier.

So before moving forward beyond the simple implementation that I have, is there any reason to do these
checks other than to identify where an issue occurs?  And is it really that useful to know where a NaN
first appears (essentially trying to identify where overflows first become an issue)?

And, ultimately, is that info sufficiently helpful that it's worth making functions harder to implement?

On Wed, Aug 27, 2014 at 1:19 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
> On Aug 26, 2014, at 6:16 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> >> The C++ spec for exp isn't ill defined!  It's clearly defined to
> >> return NaN on NaN input.
> >
> >
> > But the spec is defined on a function-by-function basis.  That's what I mean.
> >
>
> The core C++ library functions all do the same thing.  They
> all return NaN when given NaN inputs.  And they raise error
> flags.  For instance, if exp() overflows, it sets errno to
> ERANGE, indicating a range problem (i.e., value can't be
> represented in floating point).
>
> >> The main problem in not following the spec is that it means people
> >> can have code that runs with doubles and produces reasonable outputs
> >> but can't run with Nomad.  For instance, it might execute two
> >> statements and if statement a produces NaN use statement b.  This is
> >> fine and fine for auto-diff, just not an optimal way to code things.
> >
> > No it's not -- it's a discontinuous function waiting to happen.  Again, I'm
> > happy making Nomad more strict to ensure that it's also more robust.
>
> Two different kinds of robustness.  Robustness to bad derivatives
> vs. robustness to bad code.  Both sides have something to say for them,
> and I'm OK either way.
>
> >
> >> I see --- this is the same beef as with the doc Daniel's suggesting.
> >>
> >> There are two domains in play.  For exp(x), the mathematical function
> >> is defined for x in (-inf, inf) and the output is in (0,inf).   The
> >> floating-point implementation is defined for all the floating point
> >> numbers, including NaN and +/- inf.  For +inf it returns +inf,
> >> for -inf it returns 0 and for NaN it returns NaN.  Furthermore, for
> >> values outside of roughly (-800,800) it also returns NaN.
> >
> > Checking the "empirical" domain would be a pain in the ass and cause
> > no end of developer problems.  Hence the option to add an output check
> > (or more precisely, checks when trying to push values and partials onto
> > the respective stacks).
>
> Agreed.
>
> >> What's inversion?   You mean log?   Underflow's a problem if people naively
> >> multiply a bunch of probabilities together.  There's no relevant inversion
> >> anywhere.
> >
> > A probability density smaller than the smallest floating point number being represented
> > by zero is fine.  You only run into issues when you need a nonzero probability density, like
> > trying to compute the log density...
> >
> >> If you check (x + y) for x or y being NaN, that's a pretty big
> >> hit relative to the evaluation cost.
> >>
> >>> Biggest question is still unanswered -- validate inputs only (requires
> >>> very strict checks and worry about things like overflow) or just have
> >>> the inputs validated for NaNs and domain errors and check again
> >>> for any divergences in the outputs?
> >>
> >> I'd say check up front when you can and when it's not too computationally
> >> expensive.  That gives you finer granularity on reporting what went wrong.
> >> But if it's too expensive, then it's probably not worth the finer grain
> >> of reporting.
> >
> > But we're not just computing x + y -- we're also creating a node in the expression graph
> > and incrementing the stacks (which have if statements that already mess up aggressive
> > inlining).  All of the autodiff overhead would nominally make the check overhead
> > negligible.
>
> Maybe.  Only way you'll know is to profile it.
>
> Are if statements particularly bad for inlining?  I was thinking
> of them as more problematic for prefetching instructions and
> branch prediction.
>
> > I'm also not going to implement bespoke checks for every function separately.  That's
> > too much of a pain for development and testing.  If we want a robust, readily debuggable
> > stack then we're going to have to take the performance hit.
>
> How are you going to do that?  Just check the nodes getting created
> on the autodiff stack?  Will you be able to have messages saying which
> function the error came from?
>
> > Certainly no one is monitoring Stan's performance as these kinds of checks are
> > being added.
>
> You're right.  But we should be monitoring this kind of thing,
> at least with microbenchmarks.

>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
I think that's exactly the right framing of the question.

The one additional thing I'd add is fidelity of the autodiff
arithmetic to the double-based arithmetic.  Again, I'm not sure
how critical that is.  For instance, is it OK to use two different
exp() implementations?

If we wanted to make our auto-diff library most useful,
we'd have configurable behavior.  This is what both Eigen
and Boost do.  It does add a bit of complexity to use,
with Eigen's environment variable being perhaps a little
coarser but easier to use than Boost's template traits.

I also agree that programming time, and by that I include doc,
testing and maintenance is a relevant concern.   We want to
balance building the world's best autodiff library versus
actually delivering one in a finite amount of time.

C++ also sets a state-monitoring flag when arithmetic
goes bad, but it's up to the application to decide what to
do with it.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Nomad I/O Validation
messages.body_plain:
If memory serves, the issue that sparked the recent obsession with NaN was that a function was producing non-NaN outputs for a NaN input due to some special casing.  This is clearly bad behaviour and should be tested for and prevented.  I would err on the level of following C++/IEEE floating-point and just allowing NaN to propagate up and allowing a user (meaning C++ API user) to check for NaNs when/if they want rather than including explicit isnan() checks all over the place which will hurt performance (potentially quite badly) under normal, non-NaN operation.  Given that, combined with the added programming overhead that adding all of these checks (and templating them out) would add, I'd say the policy should be to allow NaNs to propagate and leave it to the user to check.

For Stan we want to catch NaNs as early as is practical to reject bad samples.  There are two (main) reasons to do this:

1. For speed, so we can stop computing the rest of the posterior function when we know it's going to be thrown out.
2. For ease of debugging, so that we can report to the user more information about where the NaN came from and why the sample was rejected.

Adding a large number of isnan() checks which slow down normal operation simply to get a small gain when we (hopefully rarely) reject a sample early seems like a loosing proposition.  Ease of debugging is a nice reason, but if we catch NaNs when, e.g., they're added to the log prob accumulator or when a distribution is computed, I think we'd still have a reasonable level of debugging information with less performance overhead.

Cheers,
Marcus
