> > >> values outside of roughly (-800,800) it also returns NaN.
> > >
> > > Checking the "empirical" domain would be a pain in the ass and cause
> > > no end of developer problems.  Hence the option to add an output check
> > > (or more precisely, checks when trying to push values and partials onto
> > > the respective stacks).
> >
> > Agreed.
> >
> > >> What's inversion?   You mean log?   Underflow's a problem if people naively
> > >> multiply a bunch of probabilities together.  There's no relevant inversion
> > >> anywhere.
> > >
> > > A probability density smaller than the smallest floating point number being represented
> > > by zero is fine.  You only run into issues when you need a nonzero probability density, like
> > > trying to compute the log density...
> > >
> > >> If you check (x + y) for x or y being NaN, that's a pretty big
> > >> hit relative to the evaluation cost.
> > >>
> > >>> Biggest question is still unanswered -- validate inputs only (requires
> > >>> very strict checks and worry about things like overflow) or just have
> > >>> the inputs validated for NaNs and domain errors and check again
> > >>> for any divergences in the outputs?
> > >>
> > >> I'd say check up front when you can and when it's not too computationally
> > >> expensive.  That gives you finer granularity on reporting what went wrong.
> > >> But if it's too expensive, then it's probably not worth the finer grain
> > >> of reporting.
> > >
> > > But we're not just computing x + y -- we're also creating a node in the expression graph
> > > and incrementing the stacks (which have if statements that already mess up aggressive
> > > inlining).  All of the autodiff overhead would nominally make the check overhead
> > > negligible.

> >
> > Are if statements particularly bad for inlining?  I was thinking
> > of them as more problematic for prefetching instructions and
> > branch prediction.
> >
> > > I'm also not going to implement bespoke checks for every function separately.  That's
> > > too much of a pain for development and testing.  If we want a robust, readily debuggable
> > > stack then we're going to have to take the performance hit.
> >
> > How are you going to do that?  Just check the nodes getting created
> > on the autodiff stack?  Will you be able to have messages saying which
> > function the error came from?
> >
> > > Certainly no one is monitoring Stan's performance as these kinds of checks are
> > > being added.
> >
> > You're right.  But we should be monitoring this kind of thing,
> > at least with microbenchmarks.
> >
> > - Bob

On Fri, Aug 29, 2014 at 10:03 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Okay, let me step back a second.  What is the point of input/output validation?

I'll second Bob's sentiment: thanks for taking a step back.

The point of input/output validation is to implement a consistent specification of our functions. In all our discussions, I'm actually surprised an alternative proposal hasn't come up: specifying preconditions. That would put the burden on the caller. I think the reason we're doing all this validation now is because we allow any double to get in and we don't want undefined behavior of our functions which would mask errors. by that, I mean generating and calling the log probability function which should have resulted in an error, but doesn't.

I'll try to outline different options: suppose we have two functions, foo(double x) and bar(double y). Let's assume we're trying to do bar(foo(x)), for some double value, x. Under all cases, bar(foo(x)) evaluates to the right thing where it's well behaved.
1. If we always checked input:
  - bar(foo(NaN)) would stop and we'd know that foo was called improperly
  - bar(foo(x)), where foo(x) evaluates to NaN, would stop and we'd know that bar was called improperly, but we wouldn't know that foo(x) wasn't run properly. Of course, if we always checked input, we shouldn't be returning NaN ever, so this case wouldn't exist.

2. If we always checked output:
  - bar(foo(NaN)) where foo(NaN) returns a NaN will report an error stating that foo didn't finish properly.
  - bar(foo(NaN)) where foo(NaN) returns a normal number will not report an error. This is where we could be in a lot of trouble.

3. If we had a bunch of preconditions, we'd need to do something like:
  - bar(foo(x)) can't be evaluated directly. We would have to do: check(x); foo(x); check(foo(x)); bar(foo(x)); But we'd have the same behavior as 1.

I think what we're doing now is trying to tighten up the spec by stating that if a function argument takes in an NaN, it must return NaN (where sensible) or it must throw an exception. It is not allowed to take NaN and then return some number like 0 or 1. This is happening now in Stan code.

I wanted to respond to Marcus's point.

On Fri, Aug 29, 2014 at 2:11 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> If memory serves, the issue that sparked the recent obsession with NaN was that a function was producing non-NaN outputs for a NaN input due to some special casing.

No, it wasn't due to special casing. Most of our issues have to do with inconsistent implementations by Boost and Eigen where an NaN input produces non-NaN output when the standard library does produce NaN.

> This is clearly bad behaviour and should be tested for and prevented.  I would err on the level of following C++/IEEE floating-point and just allowing NaN to propagate up and allowing a user (meaning C++ API user) to check for NaNs when/if they want...

That's pretty much what we've gone with.

> rather than including explicit isnan() checks all over the place which will hurt performance (potentially quite badly) under normal, non-NaN operation.

I haven't seen the isnan() check actually hurt performance by anything measurable on my machine using clang++ and O=3. Can you show where it does hurt performance and if that's the case, we can really think about how to get the flexibility in there? I'm more concerned with dev time over absolute breakneck speed because if / when this bug gets touched on, it'll take us a lot of time to hunt down.

> Given that, combined with the added programming overhead that adding all of these checks (and templating them out) would add, I'd say the policy should be to allow NaNs to propagate and leave it to the user to check.

There are two issues here:
1. Without checking, our implementation would mask input NaN and return a number (usually 0 or 1... that's based on just seeing what Boost and Eigen do with these functions).
2. Sounds like a redesign of our error handling. I'm happy to do it, but I think we need a design and some principled way to do this. I'm thinking that some checks should always be run and some should be optional. Optional ones include bounds checks on matrices and looks like isnan() except where necessary to follow spec. I'm all for it if someone comes up with a reasonable design.

> Adding a large number of isnan() checks which slow down normal operation simply to get a small gain when we (hopefully rarely) reject a sample early seems like a loosing proposition.

I'd like to see some (any) numbers that shows how much it slows down normal operation. I've done simple timings where I've commented out the checks and run the executable without seeing any difference in time over hundreds of runs. But if you've got a concrete example, then I'll take it into consideration.

> Ease of debugging is a nice reason, but if we catch NaNs when, e.g., they're added to the log prob accumulator or when a distribution is computed, I think we'd still have a reasonable level of debugging information with less performance overhead.

This is assuming that functions properly propagate NaN without checking for NaN, which is not the case. We need the check in order to propagate NaN. So under this condition, I think it's appropriate to leave it in and either return NaN or throw (depending on the function).

messages.body_plain:
So my concern with the speed hit of isnan() checks is based on profiling I did a while back where even simpler things like bound and size checks started popping up (~10%) in profiles on large models (a multivariate, latent factor stochastic volatility time series model with ~12 variates, ~3 factors and ~3000 timesteps).  If you're not seeing it, then maybe it's not a big deal, but it feels like we've made a number of design decisions lately which have trimmed performance in hopefully marginal ways but we don't have a good way of really measuring their impact in any systematic way.  That makes me nervous.

I agree that the policy should be that we require (and unit test) that all numeric functions propagate NaN through: NaN in means NaN out.  I want to applaud you and Peter for the work on going through and checking this.  For most functions this is the C++/IEEE defined behaviour so shouldn't require any explicit isnan() checks, so there shouldn't be any performance hit.  More complex functions (e.g., boost special functions) may require an explicit isnan() check, but in that case it seems unlikely to hurt.  Then, in generated models, we check for NaN where convenient and reasonably efficient based on our ability to accurately report that information to the user.

Where we may be differing is how often those NaN checks should be performed.  There is a spectrum here from checking before or after every single function call to only checking the final log_prob value.  Given that there are sometimes legitimate uses for allowing a NaN through (e.g., when using an approximation for parts of a numerically unstable function or when performing an operation on a matrix where only some values will actually be used) I would argue that checking every single function call is excessive.  Beyond that though I think there are any number of reasonable options for when and how to check for NaNs.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
To set the stage a bit — right now Nomad uses only the standard library or custom implementations,
so there’s no immediate concern about Boost and Eigen behavior (that said, it’s easy to wrap calls
to those libraries around NaN checks later).  Consequently, the NaN behavior in Nomad is consistent
and it’s a question of whether we want to isolate the source of the problem for the user.  Details
such as how the checks are done (isnan vs. checking error flags, checking inputs and/or outputs)
are second-order.

These source messages have historically been useful for both users and our own ability to debug
users’ code so I understand why we would want to keep that functionality.  The compromise is
either speed (add input and output checks in Nomad results in 5-25% slowdowns depending on
the order of the method, etc) or code complication.  For example, this is what sort would look like,

template <short autodiff_order, bool strict_smoothness>
  inline var<autodiff_order, strict_smoothness>
    sqrt(const var<autodiff_order, strict_smoothness>& input) {

    double input_val = input.first_val();
    if (unlikely(std::isnan(input_val))) throw nomad_input_error("sqrt");
    if (unlikely(input_val < 0)) throw nomad_domain_error("sqrt");

    const short partials_order = 3;
    const unsigned int n_inputs = 1;

    next_inputs_delta = n_inputs;
    next_partials_delta =
      unary_var_body<autodiff_order, partials_order>::n_partials();

    new unary_var_body<autodiff_order, partials_order>();

    double val = std::sqrt(input.first_val());

    try {
      push_dual_numbers<autodiff_order>(val);
    } catch(nomad_error& e) {
      throw nomad_output_error("sqrt");
    }

    push_inputs(input.dual_numbers());

    double d2 = 1.0 / input.first_val();

    try {
      if (autodiff_order >= 1) push_partials(val *= 0.5 * d2);
      if (autodiff_order >= 2) push_partials(val *= - 0.5 * d2);
      if (autodiff_order >= 3) push_partials(val *= - 1.5 * d2);
    } catch(nomad_error& e) {
      throw nomad_output_error("sqrt");
    }

    return var<autodiff_order, strict_smoothness>(next_body_idx_ - 1);

  }

and this is before adding a third template parameter to var to toggle the checks and
restore top speed.

It’s no problem for me to go through and add all of this, it will just make adding new
functions more of a pain for those who are not familiar with the architecture.

Another possibility brought by Marcus is to make the source identification a feature
of Stan and not Nomad by having the internal accumulator created by the parser
do checks.  Something of a compromise.

So what do people think?  Fast code with a “debug” mode that finds the source of
problems at the expense of denser code or another compromise?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Nomad I/O Validation
messages.body_plain:
There's also some confusion here in that there's two systems
under discussion, the existing autodiff and the new "nomad"
autodiff.

My only concern is ensuring the behavior on var matches that
of double.

Given the serious issue with speed, there should be a way to
turn any additional checks off.  I'm OK doing that with either
templates or environment variables --- the latter are a bit
easier conceptually on users, but they're already buying into
a lot of template complexity and a bit more is probably no big
deal.  So to that end whatever's easier to test and maintain seems
like a good idea.

An example of where we had problems was with using Eigen's
elementwise .exp() --- it didn't comply with the std C++
lib's behavior.  Now Boost is using their own specialized
exp() implementation whose name suggests it's tuned for
SSE instructions on chips and hence faster than the std version.
That's why I brought up how much compliance with the std lib
we want.

I don't think the flags are new to C++11.  If you look here:

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/exp/?kw=exp

you'll see that the earlier version of C++ also sets flags.

So the issue for compatibility is whether we should also be calling
the std::exp to make sure we set the flags the right way.

Yet another problem is that there are multiple versions of these
things built into C++, some coming in through the C lib in cmath,
some coming with no namespace, and some coming with regular includes.

I think we also had Boost's lgamma throwing
exceptions where the std lib version didn't.  I don't think
we need the templated one from Boost any more.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Nomad I/O Validation
messages.body_plain:
Two points:

Right now Nomad defines a double version and a var version of each
function in the nomad namespace to ensure that the function values
are guaranteed to be consistent.  This pattern ensures that we can
maintain consistency even if we add Eigen/Boost functions.

The template parameters are all masked by typedefs.  So we have
the default var1, var2, var3; the variants that admit non smooth
functions, var1_wild, var2_wild, var3_wild; and nominally variants
that enable all of the i/o checking, var1_debug, var2_debug, var3_debug.
Of course a power user could specify the var template parameters
explicitly, but a casual user does’t have to worry about that detail.

That won't guarantee consistency with the standard library versions
of functions for which such exists.  Which is why I keep trying to
bring up how important this feature is.  Maybe we don't need to worry
about it --- clearly Eigen wasn't too bothered.

too, like addition and multiplication?

any choice a user has to make among options adds to the complexity of
both documentation and use (as well as testing, but that's not a user
problem).  Complexity isn't just syntactic!

- Bob

>>>
>>> Given that, combined with the added programming overhead that adding all of these checks (and templating them out) would add, I'd say the policy should be to allow NaNs to propagate and leave it to the user to  check.
>>>
>>> There are two issues here:
>>> 1. Without checking, our implementation would mask input NaN and return a number (usually 0 or 1... that's based on just seeing what Boost and Eigen do with these functions).
>>> 2. Sounds like a redesign of our error handling. I'm happy to do it, but I think we need a design and some principled way to do this. I'm thinking that some checks should always be run and some should be optional. Optional ones include bounds checks on matrices and looks like isnan() except where necessary to follow spec. I'm all for it if someone comes up with a reasonable design.
>>>
>>>
>>> Adding a large number of isnan() checks which slow down normal operation simply to get a small gain when  we (hopefully rarely) reject a sample early seems like a loosing proposition.
>>>
>>> I'd like to see some (any) numbers that shows how much it slows down normal operation. I've done simple timings where I've commented out the checks and run the executable without seeing any difference in time over hundreds of runs. But if you've got a concrete example, then I'll take it into consideration.
>>>
>>>
>>> Ease of debugging is a nice reason, but if we catch NaNs when, e.g., they're added to the log prob accumulator or when a distribution is computed, I think we'd still have a reasonable level of debugging information with less performance overhead.
>>>
>>> This is assuming that functions properly propagate NaN without checking for NaN, which is not the case. We need the check in order to propagate NaN. So under this condition, I think it's appropriate to leave it in and either return NaN or throw (depending on the function).
>>>
>>>

messages.subject: Should RStan reject unknown arguments?
messages.body_plain:
I don't know what the convention is in R, but failing
silently on "inits" rather than "init" seems confusing
for users.

An intermediate solution might be to provide a clear
warning, but my preference would be to just fail if that's
not too outrageous a behavior for R.

- Bob

>

It looks like the problem is not just that the inits are on unconstrained space as opposed to constrained space, but that the inits are being generated randomly on {-2,2} instead on of 0 in unconstrained space, or as I specify them. The model runs quickly, and I can see the two major modes if I run enough chains, but id like to have control of the inits.
